cau_hoi: In which country are the famous Giza pyramids located?
giai_thich: The three large pyramids at Giza, just outside Cairo, were built around 4,500 years ago as tombs for the pharaohs. The largest pyramid belongs to Pharaoh Khufu. The ancient Greeks regarded them as one of the Seven Wonders of the World. Mexico also has pyramids, but they were built by American civilizations with different shapes and purposes.

cau_hoi: What were the kings of ancient Egypt called?
giai_thich: "Pharaoh" comes from the Egyptian word "per-aa", meaning "great house", originally referring to the palace, later used to denote the king. The Egyptians believed the pharaoh was a bridge between humans and the gods. Pharaohs often wore crowns, held a crook and flail, and wore false beards, including female pharaohs. Egypt had about 170 pharaohs over more than 3,000 years.

cau_hoi: The ancient Egyptians preserved the bodies of the dead by mummifying and wrapping them in cloth. What are such bodies called?
giai_thich: The Egyptians believed that the soul needed the body in the afterlife. The mummification process took about 70 days: organs were removed, covered in natron salt to dry, and then wrapped in hundreds of meters of linen. The brain was extracted through the nose with a hook. The Egyptians also mummified cats, crocodiles, and birds.

cau_hoi: Who was the first emperor to unify China?
giai_thich: In 221 BC, the king of Qin, Ying Zheng, conquered the other six states, unified China, and proclaimed himself "First Emperor", meaning the first emperor. He standardized writing, currency, and measurement units. His tomb is guarded by a massive army of terracotta warriors. The name "China" may derive from the word "Qin".

cau_hoi: What is the first and longest period in human history, when humans primarily made tools from stone, called?
giai_thich: The Stone Age began about 3 million years ago when human ancestors first successfully chipped stones into sharp tools, lasting until about 3000 BC in many places. It accounts for over 99% of human history. It is divided into the Paleolithic (hunting and gathering) and Neolithic (beginning agriculture and animal husbandry). This was followed by the Bronze Age and then the Iron Age.

cau_hoi: The Great Sphinx of Giza has the head of a human and the body of which animal?
giai_thich: The Sphinx is carved from a single block of limestone, about 73 meters long and 20 meters high, making it one of the largest monolithic statues in the world. The lion symbolizes strength, while the human head represents the intelligence of the pharaoh. The statue's nose has been missing for centuries, and it was not shot off by Napoleon's troops as rumored.

cau_hoi: The ancient Egyptian civilization developed along which river?
giai_thich: Egypt is mostly desert, but every year the Nile River floods, leaving behind fertile silt that helps grow wheat and barley. The historian Herodotus called Egypt "the gift of the Nile." Most ancient Egyptians, and even today, live in a narrow strip of land along both sides of the river. The Nile is one of the longest rivers in the world.

cau_hoi: What is the writing system that used pictograms in ancient Egypt called?
giai_thich: Egyptian hieroglyphics consist of over 700 symbols, including images of people, animals, and objects. Some symbols represent sounds, while others convey meanings. The writing could be read from left to right, right to left, or top to bottom, and readers knew the direction based on the orientation of human and animal figures. Cuneiform is from Mesopotamia.

cau_hoi: Which young pharaoh had a nearly intact tomb discovered in 1922, filled with treasures?
giai_thich: Tutankhamun ascended the throne at about 9 years old and died around 19. He was not a significant pharaoh, but his tomb is one of the very few royal tombs that had not been completely looted, making it the most famous. The tomb contained over 5,000 artifacts, including the famous golden mask and chariots.

cau_hoi: The region of Mesopotamia, the cradle of many ancient civilizations, lies between which two rivers?
giai_thich: "Mesopotamia" means "the land between two rivers", mostly located in present-day Iraq. Here, the Sumerians built the first cities, invented writing, the wheel, and irrigation systems. The Akkadian, Babylonian, and Assyrian empires developed in this region. It is often referred to as "the cradle of civilization."

cau_hoi: What is the only wonder of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that still exists today?
giai_thich: The Great Pyramid of Giza is the oldest wonder on the list, built around 2560 BC, and ironically, it is the only one still standing. The other six wonders were destroyed by earthquakes, fires, or wars. As for the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, it remains uncertain whether it ever existed.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the most important sun god in ancient Egyptian religion?
giai_thich: The god Ra is often depicted with a falcon head, wearing a solar disk. The Egyptians believed that each day Ra sailed across the sky, and at night traveled through the underworld, battling the giant serpent Apep to ensure the sun would rise again the next morning. Pharaohs referred to themselves as 'sons of Ra.' Zeus is a Greek god, and Odin is a Norse god.

cau_hoi: Which civilization invented the cuneiform writing system, one of the oldest writing systems in the world?
giai_thich: Around 3200 BC, the Sumerians in Mesopotamia used reed styluses to press into wet clay tablets, creating wedge-shaped marks. Initially, the writing was used to record goods such as barley and livestock. Cuneiform was used for about 3,000 years for various languages. Hundreds of thousands of clay tablets have been found, as clay becomes more durable when fired.

cau_hoi: In which kingdom was the Code of Hammurabi, one of the oldest written legal codes, created?
giai_thich: King Hammurabi of Babylon had 282 laws inscribed on a black stone stele about 2.25 meters tall, placed in a public area for everyone to see. The code regulated trade, family, wages, and punishments. At the top of the stele, there is an image of the king receiving the laws from the sun god Shamash, the god of justice.

cau_hoi: The ancient city of Babylon, home to the legendary Hanging Gardens, is located in which modern-day country?
giai_thich: The ruins of Babylon are located by the Euphrates River, about 85 km south of Baghdad. It was once one of the largest cities in the ancient world. In the 1980s, Saddam Hussein rebuilt part of the palace and inscribed his name on bricks like ancient kings. In 2019, Babylon was recognized as a World Heritage Site.

cau_hoi: Where was Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, born in Lumbini, which is now part of which country?
giai_thich: Traditionally, Prince Siddhartha was born in the Lumbini garden, near the border of present-day Nepal and India, around the 6th to 5th century BC. King Ashoka later erected a stone pillar here with an inscription stating 'The Buddha was born here.' Although born in Nepal, the Buddha attained enlightenment and taught primarily in northern India. Lumbini is a World Heritage Site.

cau_hoi: Confucius, a philosopher who greatly influenced East Asia, was from which country?
giai_thich: Confucius (551 – 479 BC) was born in the state of Lu, now part of Shandong Province, China. He taught about ethics, filial piety, propriety, and governance through virtue. His teachings were recorded by his students in the book 'Analects.' Confucianism has profoundly influenced China, Vietnam, Korea, and Japan for over 2,000 years.

cau_hoi: In which country is the ancient stone circle monument Stonehenge located?
giai_thich: Stonehenge is located in Wiltshire, southern England, and was built in several stages from around 3000 to 2000 BC. The largest stones weigh about 25 tons. The stones are aligned with the sunrise on the summer solstice and sunset on the winter solstice. The purpose of the monument remains a mystery; it may have been a site for rituals or burials.

cau_hoi: How was the Terracotta Army of Qin Shi Huang discovered in 1974?
A: Found according to an ancient map
C: A farmer accidentally found it while digging a well
D: Archaeologists used satellites to find it
giai_thich: In March 1974, a group of farmers near Xi'an discovered pottery fragments while digging a well. Archaeologists unearthed thousands of soldier, horse, and chariot figures, estimated to be around 8,000 in total. Each soldier has a different face. Initially, the figures were brightly painted, but the paint quickly flaked off when exposed to air.

cau_hoi: In which country are the famous cave paintings of Lascaux, created about 17,000 years ago, located?
giai_thich: In 1940, four teenagers following their dog discovered the Lascaux cave in southwestern France. The walls feature around 600 animal paintings such as horses, bison, and deer, painted with mineral-based colors. The cave has been closed to visitors since 1963 due to the damage caused by human breath, and tourists can now only view replicas.

cau_hoi: Who was the first person to successfully decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs using the Rosetta Stone?
giai_thich: The Rosetta Stone contains the same text written in three scripts, including ancient Greek, which scholars were able to read. The French linguist Champollion, who knew over 10 languages, compared the proper names and successfully deciphered it in 1822. It is said that when he discovered it, he ran to tell his brother and then fainted from excitement.

cau_hoi: According to legend, which Babylonian king built the Hanging Gardens of Babylon?
giai_thich: According to legend, King Nebuchadnezzar II (reigned around 605 – 562 BC) built the gardens on high terraces for his wife to remember the green mountains of her homeland. However, Babylonian texts from that time do not mention the gardens, and archaeologists have not found any traces of them. Some scholars believe the gardens may have actually been located in the city of Nineveh in Assyria.

cau_hoi: Which civilization invented the alphabet, the precursor to the Greek and Latin scripts we use today?
giai_thich: The Phoenicians, skilled maritime traders from present-day Lebanon, created an alphabet of about 22 letters that only represented consonants around 1050 BC. This alphabet was much easier to learn than the hundreds of symbols of hieroglyphs or cuneiform. The Greeks borrowed it and added vowels. The term "alphabet" comes from the first two letters: alpha and beta.

cau_hoi: Which ancient civilization used one of the first calendars with 365 days each year?
giai_thich: The Egyptians tracked the star Sirius, noticing it reappeared in the sky at dawn just as the Nile River began to flood. They divided the year into 12 months, each with 30 days, plus 5 festival days at the end of the year. This calendar served as the basis for the Julian calendar of the Romans and the modern Gregorian calendar.

cau_hoi: Which pharaoh was the Great Pyramid of Giza built as a tomb for?
giai_thich: The Pyramid of Khufu (known to the Greeks as Cheops) was built around 2560 BC. Archaeologists believe it was constructed by tens of thousands of paid workers, not slaves as many think, as they have found the workers' village with a bakery. Interestingly, the only remaining statue of Khufu is only about 7.5 cm tall.

cau_hoi: Which famous female pharaoh of Egypt is often depicted wearing male clothing and a false beard?
giai_thich: Hatshepsut ruled for about 20 years (around 1479 – 1458 BC), one of the most successful queens in history. To assert her power, she was depicted with a false beard and the attire of male pharaohs. Her reign was marked by peace and prosperity. After her death, her successor Thutmose III ordered her name to be erased and many of her statues destroyed.

cau_hoi: Who founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire, one of the largest empires of ancient times?
giai_thich: Around 550 BC, Cyrus overthrew the Media kingdom and established the Persian Empire, then conquered Lydia and Babylon. He was known for his tolerance and respect for the customs and religions of the conquered peoples. In the Bible, he is praised for allowing the Jews to return to their homeland. His empire stretched from Egypt to India.

cau_hoi: The Indus Valley Civilization, one of the oldest civilizations in the world, primarily occupied the territory of which modern-day country?
giai_thich: The Indus Valley Civilization (or Harappan Civilization) developed around 2600 – 1900 BC, primarily along the Indus River in present-day Pakistan, and partly in northwestern India. The cities were planned in a grid layout with advanced drainage systems. This was the largest civilization contemporary with ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia.

cau_hoi: According to the Bible, which shepherd boy defeated the giant Goliath with a stone and later became king of Israel?
giai_thich: According to the story, David used only a sling and a stone to strike Goliath, the giant warrior of the Philistines. Later, David became the second king of Israel, choosing Jerusalem as the capital around 1000 BC. Today, "David and Goliath" is an idiom referring to the confrontation between the underdog and a much stronger opponent. The Star of David is a symbol on the flag of Israel.

cau_hoi: What are the massive step pyramid structures of ancient Mesopotamia called?
giai_thich: Ziggurats were built of mud bricks, with multiple tiers that narrowed towards the top, featuring a small temple at the summit for the gods to descend. Unlike Egyptian pyramids, which served as tombs, ziggurats were places of worship and had no interior rooms. Many scholars believe the story of the Tower of Babel in the Bible was inspired by ziggurats in Babylon.

cau_hoi: Which Indian emperor converted to Buddhism and renounced war after witnessing the carnage in the Kalinga War?
giai_thich: Around 261 BC, King Ashoka of the Maurya Empire conquered Kalinga, resulting in approximately 100,000 deaths. Regretting his actions, he converted to Buddhism and ruled with a spirit of non-violence, inscribing moral teachings on pillars and rock faces throughout the empire. He sent monks to spread the faith across Asia. The Dharma wheel on his pillars is now at the center of the Indian national flag.

cau_hoi: The famous lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, is located in which city?
giai_thich: The Lighthouse of Alexandria (Egypt) was built around 280 BC on the island of Pharos, standing about 100 meters tall, making it one of the tallest structures in the world at that time. During the day, mirrors reflected sunlight, and at night, fires were lit to help ships navigate into the harbor. The lighthouse was gradually destroyed by several earthquakes and completely collapsed in the 14th century.

cau_hoi: The giant statue of the Sun God (Colossus), one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, stood on which island?
giai_thich: The people of Rhodes (Greece) erected a bronze statue of the Sun God Helios, approximately 33 meters tall, comparable to the Statue of Liberty (excluding the pedestal), to celebrate victory in a siege. The statue stood for about 54 years before being toppled by an earthquake in 226 BC. The image of the statue standing with legs apart at the harbor entrance is a later imagination. The term 'colossal' derives from this statue.

cau_hoi: The term 'mausoleum' in English originates from the name of whom?
D: King Mausolus, whose tomb is one of the Seven Wonders
giai_thich: Mausolus was the ruler of Caria. After his death in 353 BC, his wife commissioned a grand tomb in Halicarnassus (now Bodrum, Turkey), approximately 45 meters tall, decorated by the most famous Greek sculptors. The structure was so beautiful that it was included among the Seven Wonders, and his name became a general term for large tombs.

cau_hoi: In which year did Qin Shi Huang unify China?
giai_thich: After nearly 10 years of warfare, in 221 BC, the Qin state defeated the Qi state, the last of the six states, ending the Warring States period that lasted over 250 years. Qin Shi Huang divided the country into counties governed by officials rather than granting land to nobles. The year 206 BC marks the fall of the Qin dynasty, just about 15 years later.

cau_hoi: Taoism, with the book 'Tao Te Ching', is believed to have been founded by whom?
giai_thich: Laozi is believed to have lived around the 6th century BC, contemporaneously with Confucius. According to legend, in his old age, he rode a buffalo out of China, and a gatekeeper asked him to leave behind his teachings, leading him to write the 'Tao Te Ching' of about 5,000 words. Taoism emphasizes living in harmony with nature and 'wu wei' (non-action). The yin-yang symbol is closely associated with Taoism.

cau_hoi: Pharaoh Ramses II and the Hittites signed one of the oldest known peace treaties in the world after which battle?
giai_thich: In 1274 BC, Ramses II fought against Hittite King Muwatalli II at Kadesh (Syria), the largest chariot battle in history with thousands of chariots. The outcome was nearly a draw, although both sides claimed victory. About 15 years later, the two nations signed a peace treaty, with both Hittite and Egyptian versions still in existence. Ramses also married a Hittite princess.

cau_hoi: Which dynasty lasted the longest in Chinese history, approximately 790 years?
giai_thich: The Zhou Dynasty lasted from around 1046 to 256 BC. However, from 771 BC, the king gradually lost power, and the vassal states competed during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods. It was during this chaotic time that great thinkers like Confucius, Laozi, and Sun Tzu emerged. The Zhou introduced the concept of 'Mandate of Heaven'.

cau_hoi: Who is the author of the 'Records of the Grand Historian', the first major historical work of China?
giai_thich: Sima Qian (circa 145 – 86 BC) was a historian of the Han dynasty. After defending a defeated general, he was severely punished by Emperor Wu of Han. Instead of committing suicide like many of his contemporaries, he endured humiliation to complete the 'Records of the Grand Historian', documenting history over 2,000 years across 130 chapters. He is regarded as the 'father of Chinese historiography'.

cau_hoi: The book 'The Art of War', the most famous military treatise of ancient times, is attributed to whom?
giai_thich: Sun Tzu (Sun Wu) is believed to have lived during the Spring and Autumn period, around the 6th to 5th century BC. The book consists of 13 chapters, featuring famous quotes such as 'Know your enemy and know yourself, and you can fight a hundred battles without disaster' and 'The best victory is that which requires no battle'. Today, 'The Art of War' is still studied in military academies and even in business.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the famous gate adorned with blue glazed tiles, decorated with images of dragons and bulls, that once served as the entrance to the city of Babylon?
giai_thich: The Ishtar Gate was built by King Nebuchadnezzar II around 575 BC, dedicated to the goddess Ishtar. The shimmering blue glazed bricks sparkled in the sun, featuring hundreds of images of mushhushshu dragons and wild bulls. In the early 20th century, German archaeologists took pieces of the gate back to Berlin and reconstructed it in the Pergamon Museum.

cau_hoi: Which Greek scientist is said to have run into the street shouting "Eureka!" (I found it!) while taking a bath?
giai_thich: According to the story, King Hiero II of Syracuse suspected that his golden crown was mixed with silver. When he stepped into the bath, Archimedes noticed the water level rise and realized he could measure the volume of an object by the amount of water it displaced. By comparing it with a solid gold object of the same weight, he could determine whether the crown was mixed. This is the foundation of Archimedes' principle of buoyancy.

cau_hoi: Queen Nefertiti, famous for her stunning bust, was the wife of which pharaoh?
giai_thich: Nefertiti ("The Beautiful One Has Come") was the queen of Akhenaten, and they may have ruled together. Her painted limestone bust was discovered by a German archaeologist in 1912 in a sculptor's workshop, and it is now housed in the Neues Museum in Berlin. Egypt has repeatedly requested the return of the bust. There is a hypothesis that she was the stepmother of Tutankhamun.

cau_hoi: Pharaoh Akhenaten caused a major religious shift in Egypt by worshipping only one god. Who was that god?
giai_thich: Akhenaten (reigned circa 1353 – 1336 BC) abandoned the worship of many traditional gods like Amun, focusing solely on Aten, the sun disk with rays ending in hands. He changed his name, built a new capital, and promoted a more naturalistic artistic style. After his death, the old gods were restored, and his name was erased from many king lists.

cau_hoi: Which Han envoy opened the way to the Western Regions (Central Asia), contributing to the formation of the Silk Road?
giai_thich: In 138 BC, Emperor Wu of Han sent Zhang Qian to Central Asia to seek allies against the Xiongnu. He was captured by the Xiongnu for about 10 years, married there, then escaped and continued his journey. He returned after about 13 years, bringing information about western kingdoms and the rare "heavenly horses." This journey opened trade routes between China and the West.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the oldest existing literary work in the world, which tells the story of a king seeking immortality?
giai_thich: The Epic of Gilgamesh from Mesopotamia dates back to around 2100 BC and is inscribed on clay tablets. King Gilgamesh of Uruk, after the death of his close friend, set out to find a way to live forever. The epic includes a flood story similar to Noah's Ark in the Bible. The most complete version was found in the library of King Ashurbanipal.

cau_hoi: Who founded the Akkadian Empire, often regarded as the first empire in human history, around 2334 BC?
giai_thich: According to legend, Sargon was set adrift as a baby in a basket, found and raised by a gardener, and later became a cupbearer to the king. He overthrew the king and conquered the Sumerian city-states, establishing an empire that stretched from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean. He ruled for about 56 years and maintained a standing army of about 5,400 men.

cau_hoi: The famous library of Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, containing tens of thousands of clay tablets, was located in which city?
giai_thich: King Ashurbanipal (7th century BC) was literate, which was rare among kings of that time, and he sent people to collect texts throughout the empire. When Nineveh was destroyed in 612 BC, the fire baked the clay tablets, preserving them. British archaeologists discovered the library in the 1850s, and most of the tablets are now in the British Museum.

cau_hoi: Who began the construction of the ceremonial capital Persepolis of Persia, with its staircases carved with images of nations bringing gifts?
giai_thich: Darius I began building Persepolis around 518 BC, and his son Xerxes completed it. The reliefs on the staircases depict envoys from about 23 nations bringing gifts to the king, possibly during the Nowruz festival. In 330 BC, Alexander the Great's army burned Persepolis. The ruins in Iran are now a World Heritage site.

cau_hoi: The famous saying "Neither snow, nor rain, nor heat, nor gloom of night stays these couriers from the swift completion of their appointed rounds" by Herodotus originally described whom?
giai_thich: The Persian Empire had a system of horse stations along the Royal Road, with a station every day's journey providing fresh horses and riders ready to replace them. As a result, messages could travel about 2,700 km in just 7 to 9 days, while it took pedestrians about 90 days. Today, Herodotus' saying is inscribed on the main post office building in New York.

cau_hoi: What are the two largest cities of the ancient Indus civilization?
giai_thich: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa are both located in present-day Pakistan, each city could have around 30,000 – 40,000 people. Harappa was discovered first, so the civilization is also referred to as "Harappan civilization." Mohenjo-daro means "Mound of the Dead" in Sindhi. Interestingly, archaeologists have not found any large palaces or temples here.

cau_hoi: Which advanced structure are the cities of the Indus Valley civilization famous for that many other cities of that time did not have?
D: Underground drainage system and indoor bathrooms
giai_thich: Most houses in Mohenjo-daro had bathrooms and toilets connected to a covered drainage system running under the streets. The city also had a "Great Bath," a waterproofed pool made with natural asphalt. Bricks were fired to a standard size in a ratio of 1:2:4. Many European cities did not have a similar drainage system until the 19th century.

cau_hoi: Which period is considered the "golden age" of ancient India, when mathematics, astronomy, and literature flourished?
giai_thich: The Gupta Empire (around 320 – 550) was a time of peace and prosperity. Indian mathematicians perfected the decimal numeral system with the concept of zero, and the astronomer Aryabhata calculated the value of pi quite accurately. The poet Kalidasa created famous plays. The game chaturanga, the ancestor of chess, also emerged at the end of this period.

cau_hoi: What progressive idea about Earth did the Indian astronomer Aryabhata (5th century) propose?
B: The Sun revolves around the Earth every hour
C: The Earth is a flat surface
D: The Earth rotates around its axis
giai_thich: In 499, at the age of 23, Aryabhata wrote the book "Aryabhatiya", suggesting that the stars appear to move from east to west because the Earth rotates, similar to how a person sitting in a boat sees the trees on the shore moving backward. He also correctly explained the causes of solar and lunar eclipses. The first satellite of India launched in 1975 was named Aryabhata.

cau_hoi: Who is the advisor and author of the "Arthashastra" on the art of governance, who helped Chandragupta establish the Maurya Empire?
giai_thich: Chanakya was a Brahmin scholar, believed to have discovered and trained the young Chandragupta to overthrow the Nanda dynasty. The "Arthashastra" discusses how to manage economics, taxation, diplomacy, warfare, and even a network of spies. He is often compared to Machiavelli of Europe, but lived about 1,800 years earlier.

cau_hoi: What material were the oldest known Chinese characters from the Shang Dynasty carved on?
giai_thich: During the Shang Dynasty (around 1600 – 1046 BC), diviners carved questions onto tortoise shells and cattle shoulder bones, then heated them to observe the cracks and predict good or bad omens. The writing on these is called oracle bone script. In 1899, a scholar discovered them when he saw inscriptions on 'dragon bones' sold as traditional medicine. To date, over 150,000 pieces have been found.

cau_hoi: Who is credited with improving the paper-making technique in China in 105 AD?
giai_thich: Cai Lun was a eunuch in the Eastern Han dynasty. He made paper from tree bark, rags, old fishing nets, and hemp fibers, creating a cheaper and easier-to-write-on paper than the heavy bamboo slips or expensive silk. In fact, the Chinese had made crude paper before, but he was the one who improved and popularized this technique. Tze Sheng invented movable type printing during the Song dynasty.

cau_hoi: Which Han dynasty scientist invented the world's first earthquake detection device in 132?
giai_thich: "The seismoscope" by Zhang Heng is a bronze vessel with 8 dragons facing 8 directions, each holding a ball in its mouth, and below are 8 toads with open mouths. When an earthquake occurs, the ball in the corresponding direction falls into the mouth of the toad. There was an occasion when the device detected an earthquake while no one in the capital felt anything, and a few days later, news of the earthquake in a distant region arrived.

cau_hoi: After the fall of the Qin dynasty, who did Liu Bang defeat to establish the Han dynasty?
giai_thich: Xiang Yu was a noble of the Chu state and a brave warrior, while Liu Bang came from a small official background in a village. The two opposed the Qin dynasty and then turned to fight for control in the Han–Chu war. In 202 BC, Xiang Yu was defeated and committed suicide. Liu Bang established the Han dynasty, which lasted for about 400 years. The Chinese people today still refer to themselves as 'Han people'.

cau_hoi: The ancient Kingdom of Kush in Sudan is famous for having more pyramids than Egypt. Where is their largest pyramid located?
giai_thich: In Meroë, by the Nile River in Sudan, there are about 200 smaller, steeper, and sharper pyramids than those in Egypt. Sudan has a total of over 200 pyramids, more than Egypt. The Kingdom of Kush once conquered Egypt, and their kings became pharaohs. In 1834, an Italian explorer had many pyramids' tops destroyed in search of gold.

cau_hoi: Which ancient Phoenician city is famous for its rare purple dye made from sea snails?
giai_thich: The "Tyrian purple" dye was made from the mucus of a type of sea snail, requiring thousands of snails to dye a single garment. Due to its high cost, purple became the color of kings and Roman emperors, and at one point, only emperors were allowed to wear it. The name "Phoenicia" may derive from the Greek word meaning "purple dye." Tyre is now part of Lebanon.

cau_hoi: Which ancient people in Anatolia (Turkey) are known as one of the first to master ironworking?
giai_thich: The Hittites established a powerful empire around 1650 – 1180 BC. They were pioneers in ironworking when iron was more valuable than gold and were famous for their light chariots that could carry three people. The Hittite Empire was forgotten for nearly 3,000 years until archaeologists discovered the capital Hattusa and tens of thousands of clay tablets in the early 20th century.

cau_hoi: Which famous principle of punishment appears in the Code of Hammurabi?
B: "An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth"
giai_thich: The code stipulates that the punishment corresponds to the offense: if someone blinds another person, they will be blinded in return. However, the punishment depends on social status: harming a noble is punished much more severely than harming a slave. The code also specifies the responsibility of builders: if a house collapses and kills the owner, the builder will be executed.

cau_hoi: Why does an hour have 60 minutes and a minute have 60 seconds?
B: Because the ancient Sumerians used a base-60 counting system
C: Because the Moon has 60 large craters
giai_thich: The Sumerians counted in base-60, likely because 60 is divisible by many numbers (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30), making it convenient for dividing goods. The Babylonians inherited this counting system, and the Greeks used it in astronomy. As a result, we still divide an hour into 60 minutes, a minute into 60 seconds, and a circle into 360 degrees today.

cau_hoi: Who was the architect that designed the step pyramid of Pharaoh Djoser, the first stone pyramid in Egypt?
giai_thich: Around 2650 BC, Imhotep designed the pyramid consisting of 6 stacked steps at Saqqara, the oldest large-scale stone structure still in existence. He was also a physician, astronomer, and high-ranking official. About 2,000 years after his death, the Egyptians worshipped him as a god of medicine. He is one of the rare commoners to be deified in Egypt.

cau_hoi: "The Valley of the Kings," where many pharaohs of the New Kingdom were buried, is located near which modern Egyptian city?
giai_thich: From around 1539 BC, pharaohs stopped building pyramids and instead carved tombs deep into the cliffs on the west bank of the Nile, opposite the city of Thebes (modern-day Luxor), to avoid thieves. About 63 tombs have been found, adorned with vibrant murals. However, nearly all were robbed in ancient times, except for the tomb of Tutankhamun.

cau_hoi: Which pharaoh built the Abu Simbel temple with four giant statues at its entrance?
giai_thich: Ramses II had the temple carved into the mountainside in southern Egypt, featuring four statues of himself approximately 20 meters tall. The temple was designed so that around February 22 and October 22, sunlight would shine deep into the innermost chamber, illuminating the statues of the gods. In the 1960s, when the Aswan Dam was built, the entire temple was cut into over 1,000 blocks and relocated to a higher site about 65 meters up.

cau_hoi: The famous Library of Alexandria in ancient times was established by which dynasty?
giai_thich: The Ptolemaic kings, descendants of a general of Alexander the Great, sought to collect every book in the world. It is said that every ship entering the harbor was searched, books were copied, and the library kept the original while returning the copy. The library may have housed hundreds of thousands of scrolls. It was not destroyed in one event but gradually declined over many centuries.

cau_hoi: Who was the first person to measure the Earth's circumference quite accurately by comparing the shadows in two different cities?
giai_thich: Around 240 BC, Eratosthenes, the chief librarian of the Library of Alexandria, realized that at noon on the summer solstice, the Sun shone directly down a well in Syene (Aswan), while in Alexandria, a stick cast a shadow of about 7.2 degrees. From that angle and the distance between the two cities, he calculated the Earth's circumference to be about 40,000 km, very close to the actual figure.

cau_hoi: Which Greek mathematician is known as the "father of geometry" with his book "Elements"?
giai_thich: Euclid lived in Alexandria around 300 BC. His "Elements" consists of 13 books, building geometry from a few simple definitions and axioms, then proving each theorem rigorously. This is one of the most printed and widely read books in history, used as a textbook for over 2,000 years. The geometry we learn in school is still referred to as "Euclidean geometry."

cau_hoi: The famous theorem about right triangles "the square of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides" is named after whom?
giai_thich: Pythagoras was a Greek mathematician and philosopher from the 6th century BC, who founded a school that believed "everything is number". In fact, the Babylonians and Indians knew this rule before, but the theorem is associated with his name. He also discovered the relationship between the length of a string and the pitch of sound. His followers avoided eating beans.

cau_hoi: The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay cylinder inscribed with cuneiform, is often referred to as what due to its content about respecting conquered peoples?
A: One of the oldest "human rights declarations"
D: The first code of law for mankind
giai_thich: After conquering Babylon in 539 BC, Cyrus had it inscribed on the clay cylinder that he allowed the exiled peoples to return home and restore their temples. The cylinder was discovered in 1879 and is now in the British Museum. A replica is placed at the United Nations headquarters. Some scholars argue that calling it a "human rights declaration" is somewhat exaggerated, as it mainly praises the king.

cau_hoi: In 539 BC, after conquering Babylon, which people did Cyrus the Great allow to return home and rebuild their temple?
giai_thich: Around 586 BC, Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed Jerusalem and the First Temple, taking many Jews to Babylon, a period known as the "Babylonian Exile". Cyrus allowed them to return and rebuild the Second Temple. Therefore, in the Bible, Cyrus is one of the few non-Jewish kings praised.

cau_hoi: According to Jewish tradition, which wise king built the First Temple in Jerusalem?
giai_thich: Solomon was the son of King David, famous for his wisdom. The famous story tells of him adjudicating between two women claiming the same child by suggesting to split the baby in half, realizing the true mother was the one willing to give up her claim for the child's life. He is believed to have built the Temple around the 10th century BC. Herod was the king who later expanded the Second Temple.

cau_hoi: The Dead Sea Scrolls, containing the oldest known biblical texts, were discovered in 1947 how?
A: Archaeologists dug under the Dead Sea
B: A Bedouin shepherd boy found them in a cave
giai_thich: According to the story, a Bedouin shepherd boy threw stones into a cave in Qumran to find a lost goat and heard the sound of breaking pottery. Inside were scrolls made of leather and papyrus, handwritten and about 2,000 years old. A total of about 900 texts were found in 11 caves. The dry climate of the desert helped them survive.

cau_hoi: Which fortress on a rocky mountain by the Dead Sea was the last stronghold of the Jews against the Romans in 73-74?
giai_thich: Masada is a fortress built by King Herod on top of a rock about 400 meters high. About 960 Jews held out here. The Roman army spent months building a massive ramp to advance. According to historian Josephus, when the Romans breached the walls, they found that most of the defenders had chosen death over slavery. Masada is now a World Heritage site.

cau_hoi: The first metal coins in the world were minted around the 7th century BC in which kingdom?
giai_thich: Lydia, in western Turkey today, had a river containing much electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver. The Lydians minted electrum into coins stamped with a lion's head to ensure weight. King Croesus of Lydia later minted pure gold and silver coins. He was so wealthy that "rich as Croesus" became a saying.

cau_hoi: Which queen of Palmyra (Syria) rebelled and seized Egypt from the Romans in the 3rd century?
giai_thich: Zenobia came to power in Palmyra after her husband was assassinated around 267. She spoke many languages, rode horses, and marched with her soldiers. She expanded her territory into Egypt and much of Asia Minor. In 272, Roman Emperor Aurelian defeated her and brought her back to Rome. Today she is a symbol of heroism in Syria.

cau_hoi: The Vedas, the oldest religious texts of India, were written in which language?
giai_thich: The Vedic texts were orally transmitted for thousands of years before being recorded. Priests memorized each syllable accurately using various reading methods, so the content was preserved through many generations. Sanskrit belongs to the Indo-European language family, which is distantly related to Greek, Latin, and English. Theravada Buddhist texts were written in Pali.

cau_hoi: Besides the Mahabharata, what other great epic of India tells the story of Prince Rama rescuing his wife from the demon king?
giai_thich: The Ramayana epic tells the story of Prince Rama being exiled to the forest for 14 years. His wife, Sita, is captured by the demon king Ravana and taken to the island of Lanka. With the help of the monkey god Hanuman, Rama defeats Ravana. The Ramayana has had a profound influence on Southeast Asia, such as the Ramakien epic of Thailand and the Reamker of Cambodia, and is depicted on the walls of the Bangkok Grand Palace.

cau_hoi: What is the birth name of the Buddha?
giai_thich: Siddhartha was the prince of the Shakya clan. According to tradition, his father hid all the sufferings of life from him, but when he ventured outside the palace, he saw old people, sick people, and dead bodies. At the age of 29, he renounced the palace to seek the path to liberation from suffering. "Buddha" means "the enlightened one."

cau_hoi: Where did the Buddha attain enlightenment while meditating under the Bodhi tree?
giai_thich: After many years of unsuccessful ascetic practices, Siddhartha meditated under the Bodhi tree in Bodh Gaya (Bihar, India) and attained enlightenment at around the age of 35. This is the holiest site in Buddhism. Lumbini is where he was born, Sarnath near Varanasi is where he gave his first sermon, and Kushinagar is where he entered Nirvana.

cau_hoi: Mahavira, who lived at the same time as the Buddha, is the most important figure of which religion?
giai_thich: Jainism emphasizes the principle of "ahimsa" (non-violence towards any living being). Some Jain monks cover their mouths to avoid accidentally inhaling small insects and sweep the ground before walking. Adherents strictly follow a vegetarian diet, with many avoiding root vegetables. Gandhi was greatly influenced by the non-violence philosophy of this religion.

cau_hoi: The name "India" originates from the name of which river?
giai_thich: Ancient Indians referred to the Indus River as "Sindhu." The Persians pronounced it as "Hindu," and then the Greeks called it "Indos," leading to the name "India." The term "Hindu" (the religion) also has the same origin. Ironically, most of the Indus River today flows through Pakistan rather than India.

cau_hoi: What is the current symbol of India represented by the stone pillar with four lions facing each other from King Ashoka?
giai_thich: The lion capital at Sarnath, where the Buddha delivered his first sermon, was carved from a single block of polished sandstone around the 3rd century BCE. In 1950, it became the national emblem of India, accompanied by the motto "Truth Alone Triumphs." The emblem appears on currency notes, passports, and official documents. The Dharma wheel beneath the lions is placed in the center of the Indian national flag.

cau_hoi: During which period did the "Hundred Schools of Thought" flourish, with hundreds of philosophical schools debating vigorously in China?
A: Spring and Autumn – Warring States Period
giai_thich: From the 8th to the 3rd century BCE, the Zhou Dynasty weakened, and the vassal states fought continuously. Rulers needed talented individuals to strengthen their states, so many thinkers traveled to present their ideas. Major schools included Confucianism, Daoism, Mohism, and Legalism. This was a period that formed much of Chinese philosophical thought.

cau_hoi: Mencius, the famous Confucian thinker second only to Confucius, believed that human nature is what?
giai_thich: Mencius used the example that anyone who sees a child about to fall into a well would instinctively feel compassion, which shows that kindness is innate in every person. He also stated that "the people are precious, the ruler is light." The story of "Mencius' mother moved three times" illustrates how his mother moved three times to provide him with a good learning environment. The scholar Xunzi believed that humans are inherently evil.

cau_hoi: Han Feizi is the most representative thinker of which school, foundational for the governance of the Qin Dynasty?
giai_thich: Legalism holds that humans are inherently selfish, thus they must be governed by strict laws with clear rewards and punishments, rather than by virtue. Han Feizi was a prince of the Han state, who stuttered and thus focused on writing books. Qin Shi Huang greatly admired his works, but when he arrived in the Qin state, he was envied by his former classmate Li Si and was cruelly executed in prison.

cau_hoi: Shang Yang was a famous reformer who helped which state become powerful in the 4th century BCE?
giai_thich: Shang Yang implemented strict laws: rewarding farmers and those who achieved military success, abolishing the privileges of the nobility. To gain the people's trust in the laws, he offered a reward to anyone who moved a log from the south gate to the north gate, and he paid the reward when someone did it. The reforms helped the Qin state grow stronger, but after the patron king died, he was brutally executed by his enemies.

cau_hoi: The ancient Dujiangyan irrigation system, built in 256 BCE and still operational today, is located in which province of China?
giai_thich: Governor Li Bing and his son designed a system that divided the Min River into two branches without the need for a dam, both preventing floods and irrigating the Chengdu plains. They carved through mountains by heating the rocks and then dousing them with cold water to crack them. Thanks to this project, Sichuan became known as the "granary of heaven." This is a World Heritage Site.

cau_hoi: According to historian Sima Qian, what substance flowed in the rivers inside the tomb of Qin Shi Huang?
giai_thich: Sima Qian wrote that the tomb contained a model of the country with rivers and seas made of flowing mercury, powered by machinery. Scientists have measured the soil on the tomb mound and found unusually high levels of mercury, suggesting that the story may be true. To this day, the main tomb has not been excavated, partly due to concerns about preserving artifacts and the toxicity of mercury.

cau_hoi: How long did the Qin dynasty, the first dynasty to unify China, last?
giai_thich: The Qin ruled all of China from 221 to 206 BC. Harsh laws and heavy labor, such as building the Great Wall and the tomb, caused resentment among the people. Just about a year after Qin Shi Huang's death, the Chen Sheng – Wu Guang uprising broke out. Although short-lived, the Qin laid the foundation for a unified China for over 2,000 years.

cau_hoi: At which battle did Xiang Yu lose his final battle and commit suicide after hearing "the sound of singing from all directions of the State of Chu"?
giai_thich: In 202 BC, Xiang Yu's army was besieged at Cai Xia. At night, Han soldiers sang songs from their homeland in Chu, causing Xiang Yu's soldiers to believe their home was lost and flee. The idiom "four directions Chu song" means being completely isolated. The story between Xiang Yu and his lover Yu Ji has been adapted into the famous Peking opera "The Overlord and Yu Ji."

cau_hoi: In 9 AD, Wang Mang usurped the Han throne and established which dynasty?
giai_thich: Wang Mang was the grandson of the empress dowager, seized power, and divided the Han dynasty into Western Han and Eastern Han. He implemented bold reforms such as nationalizing land and abolishing the slave trade, earning him the title of "the revolutionary." However, the reforms failed, and he faced major floods when the Yellow River changed course. The Xin Dynasty lasted only about 15 years.

cau_hoi: What was the name of the large peasant uprising at the end of the Eastern Han dynasty in 184, which contributed to the fall of the Han dynasty?
giai_thich: Zhang Jue, the leader of a Daoist sect, gathered hundreds of thousands of peasants wearing yellow headbands to rise up with the slogan "The blue sky has died, the yellow sky will rise." Although suppressed, the uprising caused local generals to have their own armies and become stronger than the court. This is the backdrop for the novel "Romance of the Three Kingdoms."

cau_hoi: The Three Kingdoms period in China consisted of Wei, Shu, and which other state?
giai_thich: After the Eastern Han dynasty collapsed, China was divided into three states: Wei in the north (Cao Cao, Cao Pi), Shu in the southwest (Liu Bei), and Wu in the southeast (Sun Quan). This period lasted from 220 to 280. The stories of the Three Kingdoms through the novel by Luo Guanzhong are very familiar in Vietnam and many East Asian countries.

cau_hoi: Zhuge Liang (Kongming), the renowned strategist, served as the chancellor of which state during the Three Kingdoms?
giai_thich: Zhuge Liang lived in seclusion until Liu Bei visited him three times (the Three Visits to the Thatched Cottage) to invite him to help. He was the chancellor of Shu, famous for his intelligence and loyalty, believed to have invented the "wooden ox and flowing horse" to transport food supplies. The novel also tells many embellished stories about him, such as "borrowing arrows with straw boats."

cau_hoi: In the Battle of Red Cliffs in 208, which forces did the allied army of Sun Quan and Liu Bei defeat?
giai_thich: Cao Cao brought a large army south, intending to unify China. At Red Cliffs on the Yangtze River, the weaker allied forces used fire attacks to burn Cao Cao's fleet, which was tied together at the time. This defeat prevented Cao Cao from unifying the country, leading to the tripod situation of the Three Kingdoms. The battle was adapted into the famous film "Red Cliff."

cau_hoi: According to tradition, which king unified Upper and Lower Egypt, establishing the first dynasty around 3100 BC?
giai_thich: The Narmer Palette shows the king wearing both crowns: the white crown of Upper Egypt (the south) and the red crown of Lower Egypt (the north, the delta region). Later pharaohs wore a double crown combining both. Note that "Upper Egypt" is in the south, as the Nile River flows from south to north.

cau_hoi: Which city was the capital of Egypt during the Old Kingdom, when the great pyramids were built?
giai_thich: Memphis was established at the point where the Nile Valley meets the delta region, making it very convenient to govern both regions. Nearby are the Giza and Saqqara burial sites. This was one of the largest cities in the ancient world. The city of Memphis in Tennessee (USA), home to Elvis Presley, was named after this city because it is also located by a large river.

cau_hoi: Which foreign ethnic group from Asia ruled northern Egypt around the 17th – 16th century BC and brought war chariots?
giai_thich: Hyksos means "rulers from a foreign land." They ruled the Nile Delta for about 100 years. The Egyptians learned from them how to use war chariots, composite bows, and many new types of weapons. Later, Pharaoh Ahmose I expelled the Hyksos, ushering in the most powerful New Kingdom of Egypt.

cau_hoi: Which Pharaoh is referred to as the "Napoleon of Egypt" for conducting around 17 military campaigns and expanding the largest empire?
giai_thich: Thutmose III was the son of Hatshepsut's husband. After her death, he conducted many conquests, bringing Egypt control from Sudan to the Euphrates River. In the Battle of Megiddo, he daringly led his troops through a narrow gorge for a surprise attack. He also brought back many exotic plants and animals, having their images carved on temple walls like a "botanical garden."

cau_hoi: In ancient Egyptian religion, which god ruled the afterlife and judged the souls of the dead?
giai_thich: According to mythology, Osiris was killed and dismembered by his brother Seth. His wife, Isis, found and reassembled his body, and Osiris resurrected to become the king of the afterlife. He is often depicted with green skin, symbolizing rebirth like plants growing back after the Nile floods. His son is the falcon god Horus.

cau_hoi: In the Egyptian judgment ceremony for the dead, what was the heart weighed against?
C: The heart of a sacred bull
D: The feather of the goddess Maat
giai_thich: Maat is the goddess of truth and justice. If the heart was heavier than the feather due to sins, it would be devoured by the monster Ammit, with the head of a crocodile, the body of a lion, and the hindquarters of a hippopotamus, and the soul would not continue to exist. If the heart was light, the soul would enter the beautiful Field of Reeds. Thus, the heart was the only organ left in the mummified body.

cau_hoi: Which Egyptian god has a jackal head, is the god of mummification, and the protector of tombs?
giai_thich: Jackals often roamed around cemeteries at the edge of the desert, so the Egyptians chose them as the image of the god who protects the dead. Anubis is black, the color of fertile silt and rebirth. Embalmers could wear Anubis masks during rituals. Horus has a falcon head, Thoth a ibis head, and Sobek a crocodile head.

cau_hoi: "The Book of the Dead" of ancient Egyptians is actually what?
C: A collection of spells to help the soul transition to the afterlife
giai_thich: The Egyptians believed that after death, the soul had to pass through many challenges and gates guarded by monsters. The spells were written on papyrus scrolls and placed in the coffin to help the soul answer correctly and pass the judgment. Wealthy families could commission very long scrolls with beautiful illustrations. Its original name is "The Book of Going Forth by Day."

cau_hoi: Papyrus, the primary writing material of ancient Egyptians, is made from what?
A: The stalks of papyrus plants growing along the Nile
giai_thich: The Egyptians cut the core of the papyrus stalk into thin strips, layered them in two perpendicular directions, then pressed and dried them. The natural resin in the plant helped the strips stick together. The sheets were glued together to form long rolls. The word "paper" in English comes from "papyrus." Egypt exported papyrus throughout the Mediterranean.

cau_hoi: The ancient Egyptians divided a year into three seasons based on what phenomenon?
D: The flooding cycle of the Nile
giai_thich: The three seasons are: Akhet (the flood season, when the Nile overflows), Peret (the planting season, when the water recedes leaving fertile silt), and Shemu (the harvest season). During the flood season, farmers could not work the fields, so many went to work on construction projects for the pharaoh. The Nile has not flooded annually since the Aswan High Dam was built in 1970.

cau_hoi: Who is the British archaeologist who discovered the tomb of Tutankhamun in 1922?
giai_thich: Howard Carter searched the Valley of the Kings for many years with funding from Lord Carnarvon. On November 4, 1922, the first step was found. When looking through a hole by candlelight, when asked if he saw anything, Carter replied: "Yes, wonderful things!" Lord Carnarvon died a few months later from an infection, giving rise to the legend of the "pharaoh's curse."

cau_hoi: How much does the famous gold mask of Tutankhamun weigh?
giai_thich: The mask is made of two layers of gold, inlaid with precious stones like lapis lazuli, quartz, and colored glass, weighing about 10 kg. It was placed directly on the mummy's face. In 2014, the mask's beard broke while being cleaned and was hastily glued back on, causing a scandal. Later, experts carefully repaired it. This is one of the most famous artifacts in the world.

cau_hoi: When it was first built, how tall was the Great Pyramid of Khufu, which held the record for the tallest man-made structure in the world for about 3,800 years?
giai_thich: Initially, the pyramid was about 146 meters tall, covered with a layer of polished white limestone that reflected sunlight. The outer casing and the apex were later removed to build the city of Cairo, so today the pyramid stands at about 138 meters. It was only surpassed when Lincoln Cathedral in England was built with a taller spire around 1311.

cau_hoi: Approximately how many blocks of stone were used to build the Great Pyramid of Khufu?
giai_thich: Each block of stone weighed about 2.5 tons on average, with some weighing up to about 80 tons. If built over approximately 20 years, workers would have to place about one block every few minutes, day and night. The method of transporting the stones is still debated: it may have involved sledges on watered sand and ramps. A papyrus diary of a stone carrier was found in 2013.

cau_hoi: King Gilgamesh, the main character of the oldest epic in the world, ruled which Sumerian city?
giai_thich: Uruk may have been the first large city in the world, with about 40,000 – 80,000 people around 2900 BC, and it is where cuneiform writing originated. Gilgamesh may have been a real king around 2700 BC, later mythologized. According to the epic, he had walls built that were about 9 km long. The name Iraq may derive from Uruk.

cau_hoi: What tool did the Sumerians use to write cuneiform, and on what material?
C: Reed stylus on wet clay tablets
giai_thich: The writer, known as a scribe, used the pointed end of a reed to press into wet clay, creating wedge-shaped marks. The clay tablets were dried or baked to preserve them. Boys attended 'tablet schools' from a young age and studied for many years. Archaeologists have found even homework with mistakes from Sumerian students.

cau_hoi: In which century did King Hammurabi rule Babylon?
giai_thich: Hammurabi ruled from about 1792 – 1750 BC, which is around 3,800 years ago. He transformed Babylon from a small city-state into the center of a large kingdom in Mesopotamia. In addition to his famous code of laws, he also built canals, temples, and city walls. Many letters he sent to officials still exist, showing he cared about even small issues in his kingdom.

cau_hoi: In what year was the city of Nineveh, the capital of the Assyrian Empire, destroyed by the Babylonian and Media coalition?
giai_thich: Assyria was once the most feared military empire of ancient times, known for its professional army and siege techniques. However, after the death of King Ashurbanipal, the empire weakened due to civil war. In 612 BC, the coalition attacked and burned Nineveh. The city was so abandoned that about 200 years later, when passing through, Greek historians did not recognize it as a former great capital.

cau_hoi: Which city was the main administrative center of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, the endpoint of the Royal Road?
giai_thich: Susa, located in southwestern Iran, was the capital of the ancient Elamite kingdom. Darius I built a large palace here with colored tiles. The Royal Road, about 2,700 km long, connected Susa to the city of Sardis in Asia Minor. In the Bible, the story of Queen Esther takes place in Susa. Persia had many capitals, with Persepolis primarily used for ceremonies.

cau_hoi: What was the elite army of 10,000 men of the Persian kings, always replenished as soon as someone died, called by the Greeks?
giai_thich: According to Herodotus, when a soldier died or was injured, another immediately replaced him, so the number always remained 10,000, as if they never died. They were infantry armed with spears, bows, and willow shields, with 1,000 of them being spear bearers with golden balls. The Immortals fought at the Battle of Thermopylae against 300 Spartan warriors.

cau_hoi: Who was the last king of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, defeated by Alexander the Great?
giai_thich: Darius III was defeated by Alexander twice, at the Battle of Issus (333 BC) and the Battle of Gaugamela (331 BC). At Issus, he fled, leaving behind his mother, wife, and daughter, and Alexander treated them with great respect. In 330 BC, while fleeing, Darius III was killed by his own officials. Alexander held a royal funeral for him.

cau_hoi: The Parthian Empire in Persia was famous for which military tactic that troubled the Roman army?
B: Horseback archers pretending to retreat while turning back to shoot arrows
giai_thich: Parthian cavalry could turn around on galloping horses to shoot arrows backward, known as the 'Parthian shot.' In 53 BC, at the Battle of Carrhae, they annihilated the army of Crassus, one of the three members of the Roman Triumvirate. In English, 'parting shot' may derive from 'Parthian shot.'

cau_hoi: What is the characteristic of the writing system of the Indus Valley civilization today?
A: It has been completely deciphered thanks to a trilingual stone tablet
D: Has not been deciphered by anyone yet
giai_thich: Archaeologists have found thousands of small seals with inscriptions, but each line of text is usually very short, averaging only about 5 symbols. There is no bilingual text like the Rosetta Stone for comparison. Therefore, we still do not know what language the Indus people spoke. There is a large prize for anyone who can decipher this script.

cau_hoi: What was the ancient name of the capital of the Maurya Empire, now the city of Patna in India?
giai_thich: Pataliputra, located on the banks of the Ganges River, was once one of the largest cities in the ancient world. The Greek envoy Megasthenes described the city as having a wooden wall over 30 km long with about 570 watchtowers and 64 gates. This was the capital of both Chandragupta and Ashoka. Most of the ancient city now lies deep beneath the modern city of Patna.

cau_hoi: Which son did King Ashoka send to spread Buddhism in Sri Lanka?
giai_thich: Around 250 BC, Mahinda, the son of Ashoka, became a monk and went to Sri Lanka, converting King Devanampiya Tissa. Later, his sister, nun Sanghamitta, brought a branch of the Bodhi tree under which the Buddha attained enlightenment. From Sri Lanka, Theravada Buddhism spread to Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, and Cambodia. The full moon day in June is celebrated as Poson in Sri Lanka to commemorate this event.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the oldest Vedic text, consisting of over 1,000 hymns?
giai_thich: The Rig Veda was composed around 1500 – 1000 BC and is one of the oldest religious texts still in use today. The hymns praise deities such as Indra (the god of thunder) and Agni (the god of fire). The Rig Veda contains 1,028 hymns. In 2007, UNESCO included the handwritten manuscripts of the Rig Veda in the Memory of the World Register.

cau_hoi: In the caste system of ancient India, what is the highest caste, consisting of priests and scholars, called?
giai_thich: Ancient Indian society was divided into four castes: Brahmins (priests), Kshatriyas (kings and warriors), Vaishyas (merchants and farmers), and Shudras (laborers). In addition to these four castes, there were those considered "untouchables," who faced severe discrimination. The Indian Constitution of 1950 prohibited caste discrimination.

cau_hoi: Where was the capital of the Eastern Han dynasty located, given that the Western Han dynasty was based in Chang'an?
giai_thich: After overthrowing the Xin dynasty of Wang Mang, Liu Xiu restored the Han dynasty in 25 AD and chose Luoyang, east of Chang'an, as the capital. Thus, it is called the Eastern Han. Luoyang is one of the oldest capitals in China, having served as the capital for 13 dynasties. The city is famous for its peonies and the Longmen Grottoes.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the first Buddhist temple in China, built during the Eastern Han dynasty?
giai_thich: According to legend, Emperor Ming of Han dreamed of a golden man flying in the sky, which was interpreted as the Buddha. He sent envoys to search for him, and in 68 AD, two Indian monks riding a white horse brought Buddhist scriptures to Luoyang. The emperor ordered the construction of a temple and named it White Horse in memory of the horse. Shaolin Temple was built about 400 years later.

cau_hoi: In 220 AD, Cao Pi deposed the last emperor of the Han dynasty and established which state?
giai_thich: Cao Pi was the son of Cao Cao. After his father's death, he forced Emperor Xian of Han to abdicate, officially ending the Han dynasty after about 400 years. The state of Wei occupied the vast and populous northern region. Shortly thereafter, Liu Bei and Sun Quan also declared themselves emperors, marking the beginning of the Three Kingdoms period. Later, the Wei state was usurped by the Sima family.

cau_hoi: The Daoist philosopher Zhuangzi is famous for the story of dreaming he became which animal?
giai_thich: Zhuangzi recounts that he dreamed he was a butterfly flying joyfully. Upon waking, he was unsure whether he was Zhuangzi dreaming he was a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming he was Zhuangzi. The story raises questions about the boundary between dreams and reality. He is known for his humorous writing style, full of parables, and for advocating freedom and spontaneity.

cau_hoi: The naturally mummified "Ötzi, the Iceman" approximately 5,300 years old was found in which mountain range in 1991?
giai_thich: Two German climbers discovered Ötzi in ice at the Austria-Italy border. Initially, they thought it was the body of a recently deceased climber. Ötzi carried a copper axe, a bow and arrows, a bag of medicinal herbs, and had over 60 tattoos. Scientists found an arrowhead in his shoulder, indicating he was murdered. Ötzi is displayed in a museum in Bolzano, Italy.

cau_hoi: Göbekli Tepe, the stone temple complex that may be the oldest in the world, built around 9,500 BC, is located in which country?
giai_thich: Göbekli Tepe features T-shaped stone pillars up to 5-6 meters tall, carved with images of foxes, snakes, and wild boars, constructed about 6,000 years before Stonehenge. Remarkably, it was built by hunter-gatherers, before agriculture. This discovery has led scientists to reconsider the idea that agriculture must have preceded the construction of temples.

cau_hoi: Which city is considered one of the oldest continuously inhabited places in the world, with stone walls dating back to around 8,000 BC?
giai_thich: Jericho, located near the Jordan River at about 250 meters below sea level, is one of the lowest cities in the world. Archaeologists have found a stone tower about 8.5 meters high and walls dating back approximately 10,000 years. In the Bible, the walls of Jericho fell after the Israelites blew their trumpets. Jericho is now part of Palestinian territory.

cau_hoi: The famous fossil skeleton "Lucy," belonging to a human ancestor that lived about 3.2 million years ago, was discovered in which country in 1974?
giai_thich: Lucy belonged to the species Australopithecus afarensis, standing about 1.1 meters tall. The pelvis and leg bones indicate she walked upright on two legs, even though her brain was still small like that of apes. The name Lucy was given after the Beatles song "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds," which the archaeological team played during their celebration. In Ethiopia, she is known as "Dinkinesh," meaning "You are marvelous."

cau_hoi: Which ancient human species is called "handy man" because it is believed to be one of the first to make stone tools?
giai_thich: Homo habilis lived in Africa about 2.4 to 1.4 million years ago. The name was given in 1964 by archaeologist Louis Leakey because the fossils were found near simple stone tools. Today, scientists know that stone tools existed even before this species. Homo erectus ("upright man") was the first to leave Africa, while Homo sapiens are modern humans.

cau_hoi: The Neanderthal fossil was first identified in 1856 in a valley in which country, and this ancient human species was named after that valley?
giai_thich: Limestone quarry workers in the Neander Valley near Düsseldorf discovered strange bone fragments. Neanderthals lived in Europe and Western Asia about 400,000 to 40,000 years ago, had brains equal to or larger than modern humans, knew how to use fire, and buried their dead. DNA studies show that most non-Africans today carry about 1-2% Neanderthal genes.

cau_hoi: "The Neolithic Revolution," one of the greatest turning points in human history, refers to what?
B: The transition of humans to farming and herding, living in settled communities
giai_thich: Around 10,000 to 12,000 years ago, humans in the Middle East began cultivating wheat, barley, and raising goats and sheep. Instead of moving with herds of animals, they settled into villages. Surplus food led to population growth, and craftsmen, merchants, and priests emerged. Agriculture also developed independently in China (rice, millet), the Americas (corn), and New Guinea.

cau_hoi: The "Fertile Crescent," where agriculture first emerged in the world, is located in which area?
giai_thich: The crescent-shaped region stretches from Egypt, through Israel, Lebanon, Syria to Iraq and western Iran, where fertile land and water from major rivers are found. Many wild plants and animals that are easy to domesticate, such as wheat, barley, lentils, goats, sheep, and cattle, grow here. The name was coined by American archaeologist James Henry Breasted in 1916.

cau_hoi: Which animal is believed to be the first to be domesticated by humans, tens of thousands of years ago?
giai_thich: Dogs were domesticated from gray wolves, possibly around 15,000 to over 20,000 years ago, when humans were still living by hunting and gathering, before agriculture. It is possible that less fearful wolves lingered around camps to eat leftover food, eventually living alongside humans. In Israel, a grave about 12,000 years old was found with a human buried alongside a puppy.

cau_hoi: The Bronze Age is named after the bronze alloy. This alloy is created by mixing copper with which metal?
giai_thich: Pure copper is quite soft, but when mixed with about 10% tin, it becomes much harder, suitable for making weapons, tools, and statues. Because tin is rare, countries had to engage in long-distance trade to obtain it, for example, from the Cornwall region (England) to the Mediterranean. The Đông Sơn bronze drums of Vietnam were also cast from bronze alloy.

cau_hoi: Where were the smaller "blue stones" at Stonehenge transported from, over 200 km away?
giai_thich: Geologists have identified about 80 blue stones, each weighing 2-5 tons, coming from the Preseli Hills in Wales. Neolithic people, who had no wheels or metal, transported them over 200 km. In 2024, scientists also discovered that the "Altar Stone" at the center of Stonehenge came from as far as Scotland, about 700 km away.

cau_hoi: In which country is the Altamira Cave with its famous prehistoric bison paintings located?
giai_thich: In 1879, an 8-year-old girl named María, accompanied by her father, explored the cave and looked up to see the ceiling covered with bison images. Her father, Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola, announced the discovery, but many scientists did not believe prehistoric people could paint so beautifully and accused him of forgery. It wasn't until the early 20th century, when other caves were discovered, that he was vindicated, but by then he had passed away.

cau_hoi: In 356 BC, who set fire to the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, one of the Seven Wonders, just to make his name famous?
giai_thich: Herostratus admitted that he burned the temple to ensure his name would be remembered forever. The Ephesus authorities ordered that no one mention his name, but historians still recorded it. Coincidentally, according to legend, Alexander the Great was born on the very night the temple was burned. Today, the term 'Herostratus syndrome' refers to doing something bad to gain fame.

cau_hoi: Which sculptor created the massive statue of Zeus at Olympia, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World?
giai_thich: Phidias sculpted the statue of Zeus seated on a throne, approximately 12 meters tall, with a wooden frame covered in ivory (for the skin) and gold (for the robe). It is said that if Zeus stood up, his head would pierce the temple's roof. Phidias was also responsible for the sculptures of the Parthenon in Athens. His workshop in Olympia has been discovered by archaeologists.

cau_hoi: On which island was the Lighthouse of Alexandria built, and what is the name of the island that later became the word for 'lighthouse' in many languages?
giai_thich: Pharos is a small island in front of Alexandria's harbor, connected to the mainland by a causeway. The lighthouse was so famous that the name of the island became the word for lighthouse: 'phare' in French, 'faro' in Italian and Spanish. In 1994, divers found hundreds of stone blocks and statues on the seabed nearby, possibly remnants of the lighthouse.

cau_hoi: Which Egyptian god is primarily worshipped at the massive Karnak temple complex in Luxor?
giai_thich: Karnak was built and expanded over approximately 2,000 years by around 30 pharaohs, making it one of the largest religious complexes in the world. The Hypostyle Hall has 134 massive stone columns, many of which are about 21 meters tall. Amun is known as the 'king of the gods' and is often combined with the sun god Ra to form Amun-Ra. Karnak once had thousands of priests and owned vast lands.

cau_hoi: Which dynasty did the Kushite kings, such as King Piye, establish after conquering Egypt?
giai_thich: Around 727 BC, King Piye from Nubia (Sudan) moved north to conquer Egypt. The Kushite kings ruled Egypt for about 100 years and were known as the 'black pharaohs.' They greatly respected Egyptian culture, restoring old temples and building pyramids as tombs in their homeland. They were driven back to Nubia by the Assyrians around 656 BC.

cau_hoi: Which people created the giant stone statues of human heads (moai) on Easter Island?
giai_thich: Easter Island (Rapa Nui) is one of the most remote inhabited islands in the world, belonging to Chile. The Polynesians arrived here by boat and carved nearly 1,000 moai statues, mainly between 1250 and 1500, possibly to honor their ancestors. The statues average about 4 meters tall, with some weighing over 80 tons. Legends say the statues 'walked' to their locations, and experiments have shown they could be moved using ropes in a rocking motion.

cau_hoi: How did ancient Polynesians, who settled on scattered islands across the Pacific, navigate at sea?
A: By following warm ocean currents of different colors
B: By observing stars, ocean waves, winds, and flying birds
giai_thich: Polynesians traveled in large double-hulled canoes across thousands of kilometers of ocean. They memorized the rising and setting positions of hundreds of stars, felt the direction of waves through the hull of the canoe, and observed clouds and the flight paths of seabirds to find land. This knowledge was passed down orally through generations. In 1976, the canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti using only traditional methods.

cau_hoi: Which ancient European people celebrated the festival of Samhain, from which Halloween originated?
giai_thich: The Celts in Ireland, Scotland, and surrounding areas held the Samhain festival around November 1, marking the end of the harvest season and the beginning of the dark winter. They believed that on this night the boundary between the living and the dead blurred, so they lit fires and wore costumes. Irish immigrants brought the tradition to America, where pumpkins were used instead of turnips to make lanterns.

cau_hoi: In ancient Celtic society, what were the priests, healers, and keepers of knowledge called?
giai_thich: Druids had to memorize a vast amount of knowledge about law, religion, astronomy, and herbal medicine, which could take up to 20 years, as they did not write things down. They were respected and could adjudicate disputes. Much of what we know about them comes from accounts by Romans like Julius Caesar, so it may not be entirely accurate.

cau_hoi: Which animal did the ancient Egyptians consider sacred, associated with the goddess Bastet, to the extent that harming it could lead to the death penalty?
giai_thich: Cats helped protect grain stores from mice and killed venomous snakes, making them highly revered by the Egyptians. The goddess Bastet has a cat's head and is the protector of the home. According to Herodotus, when a household cat died, the entire family would shave their eyebrows in mourning. Archaeologists have found hundreds of thousands of mummified cats in the temples of Bastet.

cau_hoi: Which sacred insect in Egyptian religion symbolizes the rising Sun and rebirth, often made into amulets?
giai_thich: The scarab rolls large dung balls on the ground. The Egyptians associated it with the god Khepri rolling the Sun across the sky each morning. The larvae emerging from the dung ball seemed to be born from nothing, symbolizing rebirth. Scarab amulets were placed on the chests of mummies. Scientists have also discovered that scarabs use the light of the Milky Way for navigation.

cau_hoi: The Egyptian unit of length 'cubit' and many other ancient peoples was based on which part of the body?
D: From the elbow to the tip of the middle finger
giai_thich: The cubit is about 52 cm (Egyptian royal cubit). Since each person's arm length varies, the Egyptians made standard measuring rods from stone or wood. The pyramids were built with high precision thanks to this standard unit of measurement. In the Bible, Noah's Ark is described as being 300 cubits long. Many ancient peoples used body parts for measurement.

cau_hoi: How many degrees did the ancient Babylonians divide a circle into, a division still used today?
giai_thich: The Babylonians used a base-60 counting system. The number 360 is close to the number of days in a year and is divisible by many numbers (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12...), making it very convenient for calculations. Each degree is further divided into 60 minutes and each minute into 60 seconds. Greek astronomers like Ptolemy inherited this division, and it is used worldwide.

cau_hoi: Which Greek philosopher is believed to have accurately predicted a solar eclipse in 585 BC?
giai_thich: Thales of Miletus is often regarded as the first Greek philosopher, as he explained the world through natural reasoning rather than deities. According to Herodotus, the eclipse he predicted occurred during a battle between the Lydians and the Medes, causing both sides to panic and make peace. There is a story that he fell into a well while gazing at the stars.

cau_hoi: Which Greek physician is known as the 'Father of Medicine,' with an oath that doctors still recite today?
giai_thich: Hippocrates (c. 460 – 370 BC) believed that diseases had natural causes rather than being divine punishments. He carefully observed patients and recorded symptoms. The 'Hippocratic Oath' requires doctors to help the sick and 'first, do no harm,' although this exact phrase does not appear in the oath. Galen was a prominent physician during Roman times.

cau_hoi: Which Greek philosopher was the first to propose the idea that all matter is made up of indivisible particles called 'atoms'?
giai_thich: Democritus (c. 460 – 370 BC) believed that everything is made up of very small particles, differing in shape and size, moving in empty space. 'Atomos' in Greek means 'uncuttable.' Aristotle opposed this idea, and his views dominated for about 2,000 years until John Dalton developed modern atomic theory in 1803.

cau_hoi: Archimedes was killed by a Roman soldier when the Romans captured which city in 212 BC?
giai_thich: Archimedes lived in Syracuse on the island of Sicily. During the siege, he designed stone-throwing machines and a giant crane with a hook, said to lift Roman ships out of the water. When the city was captured, according to legend, he was drawing figures in the sand and told the soldier, 'Do not disturb my circles!' before being killed. The Roman general in charge wanted to capture him alive and was very regretful.

cau_hoi: Chandragupta Maurya, the founder of the Maurya Empire, is said to have renounced the throne and followed which religion at the end of his life?
giai_thich: According to Jain tradition, around 297 BC, Chandragupta abdicated in favor of his son, followed a Jain teacher to southern India, lived as a monk in Shravanabelagola, and fasted to death. His grandson Ashoka converted to Buddhism. Thus, three generations of the Maurya family are associated with three different religions, as his son was linked to another sect.

cau_hoi: The large ziggurat in the city of Ur built by the Sumerians was dedicated to which god?
giai_thich: The Ziggurat of Ur was built by King Ur-Nammu around the 21st century BC and is the best-preserved ziggurat. The Moon God Nanna (called Sin by the Akkadians) is the patron deity of the city of Ur. In the 1920s and 1930s, archaeologist Leonard Woolley excavated in Ur and found royal tombs filled with gold and silver. According to the Bible, Abraham came from Ur.

cau_hoi: At the end of the Bronze Age, which language did kings from Egypt to Mesopotamia commonly use to write diplomatic letters to each other?
giai_thich: Akkadian, the language of Babylon and Assyria, written in cuneiform script, was the international diplomatic language of that time, much like English today. Scribes in Egypt had to learn Akkadian to read and respond to letters from foreign kings. Even correspondence between the Pharaoh and the Hittite king used this language.

cau_hoi: Which ancient civilization in southwestern Iran, with its capital at Susa, was a long-standing rival of the Mesopotamian kingdoms?
