giai_thich: The Elamite civilization emerged around 3200 BC, contemporaneously with Sumer, and had its own language unlike any other known language. The Elamites frequently attacked Mesopotamia, even bringing the stele of Hammurabi back to Susa as a trophy, where French archaeologists discovered it in 1901. Elam was devastated by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal around 647 BC.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the capital of the Hittite Empire, where tens of thousands of clay tablets were found?
giai_thich: Hattusa, located in central Turkey, was surrounded by a wall approximately 6 km long with lion gates and sphinx gates. Archaeologists found about 30,000 clay tablets, including the Hittite version of the peace treaty with Egypt. The city was abandoned and burned around 1180 BC. Hattusa is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cau_hoi: Which Pharaoh defeated the 'Sea Peoples' when they attacked Egypt around 1177 BC?
giai_thich: Around 1200 – 1150 BC, many Bronze Age civilizations collapsed almost simultaneously, such as the Hittites and Mycenaeans. The 'Sea Peoples' were mysterious maritime groups that attacked many Mediterranean regions. Ramses III defeated them in a battle on land and at sea, which is inscribed on the walls of the Medinet Habu temple. The causes of the Bronze Age collapse are still debated.

cau_hoi: According to legend, which queen founded the city of Carthage after fleeing from Tyre?
giai_thich: Legend has it that Dido asked the local king for a piece of land 'as much as a bull's hide.' She cleverly cut the hide into very thin strips, stitched them together, and enclosed an entire hill, where she built the city of Carthage. In Virgil's epic Aeneid, Dido falls in love with the Trojan hero Aeneas and commits suicide when he leaves. The story has inspired many operas.

cau_hoi: Which Carthaginian navigator Hanno, around the 5th century BC, sailed to explore which coastline?
giai_thich: Hanno led a large fleet across the Strait of Gibraltar and south along the West African coast to establish settlements. His voyage records mention volcanic eruptions and furry creatures that the translator called 'gorillas.' This led to the naming of the gorilla species in 1847. Researchers still debate how far he traveled.

cau_hoi: According to the Bible, whose feast was interrupted by the story of 'the mysterious hand writing on the wall' that foretold the fall of Babylon?
giai_thich: Belshazzar was the son and co-regent with King Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon. During a feast, a hand appeared writing mysterious words on the wall. The prophet Daniel interpreted that the kingdom would be divided and given to the Medes and Persians. That night, Babylon fell. The phrase 'the writing on the wall' today refers to a sign of impending doom.

cau_hoi: The Achaemenid Persian Empire divided its territory into provinces, each governed by a satrap. What were these provinces called?
giai_thich: Darius I divided the empire into about 20 – 30 satrapies. Each satrap (governor) collected taxes and maintained order, but there were other officials overseeing them, called 'the king's eyes and ears,' to prevent satraps from rebelling. The peoples retained their own languages, religions, and customs. This organization helped the vast multi-ethnic empire endure for about 200 years.

cau_hoi: Which Persian king completed the ancient canal connecting the Nile River to the Red Sea, the ancient precursor to the Suez Canal?
giai_thich: Pharaoh Necho II had begun digging the canal but left it unfinished. After Persia conquered Egypt, Darius I completed the canal connecting a branch of the Nile to the Red Sea, and erected a stone inscription stating that ships could travel directly from Egypt to Persia. This canal was repaired and used by many subsequent dynasties for centuries before being silted up.

cau_hoi: The 'qanat' system, tunnels that lead groundwater from the foothills to farmland over tens of kilometers, was invented by which people?
giai_thich: The Persians invented the qanat system around 3,000 years ago to bring groundwater to arid lands without evaporation under the sun. The tunnels are gently sloped for gravity flow, with a series of vertical shafts for ventilation and maintenance. Some qanats in Iran are several kilometers long and are still in use today. This technique spread to North Africa, Spain, and even the Americas.

cau_hoi: Which religion was King Kanishka of the Kushan Empire (2nd century) famous for patronizing?
giai_thich: The Kushan Empire controlled the regions of Afghanistan, Pakistan, and northern India, located right on the Silk Road. King Kanishka is believed to have organized a great council to compile Buddhist scriptures, and during his reign, Mahayana Buddhism flourished, spreading to Central Asia and China through merchants. His coins featured both the Buddha and Greek, Persian, and Indian deities.

cau_hoi: The Gandhara art (in present-day Pakistan – Afghanistan) is famous for combining the styles of which cultures?
giai_thich: After the conquests of Alexander the Great, many Greeks settled in this region. Gandhara artists sculpted Buddha statues with faces resembling the god Apollo, curly hair, and draped garments similar to Greek statues. This may be one of the first places where the Buddha was depicted in human form. The two giant Buddha statues in Bamiyan (Afghanistan) were influenced by this style and were destroyed in 2001.

cau_hoi: The play "Shakuntala", a masterpiece of Sanskrit literature, was written by which poet during the Gupta period?
giai_thich: Kalidasa is regarded as the greatest poet and playwright of Sanskrit literature, often referred to as the "Shakespeare of India". "Shakuntala" tells the story of the love between King Dushyanta and the girl Shakuntala, who is forgotten by the king due to a curse. When translated into European languages in the late 18th century, the play greatly impressed the German literary giant Goethe.

cau_hoi: The game of chess originated from the game chaturanga of which country around the 6th century?
giai_thich: "Chaturanga" in Sanskrit means "four divisions" of the ancient Indian army: infantry, cavalry, elephants, and chariots, which became pawns, knights, bishops, and rooks. The game spread to Persia (called shatranj), and then to Europe via the Arabs. The term "checkmate" originates from the Persian "shah mat", meaning "the king is helpless".

cau_hoi: The Ajanta caves, with their beautiful murals and Buddhist sculptures dating back about 2,000 years, are located in which country?
giai_thich: About 30 caves in Ajanta (Maharashtra state) were carved into a horseshoe-shaped rock along a river, from around the 2nd century BC to the 5th – 6th centuries. Monks used them as places for meditation and worship. The caves were covered by forest and forgotten for over 1,000 years until 1819 when a British officer hunting tigers accidentally discovered them.

cau_hoi: The Great Stupa of Sanchi, one of the oldest Buddhist structures in India, was originally built by whom?
giai_thich: Ashoka built the first stupa at Sanchi in the 3rd century BC to house the relics of the Buddha. Later, the stupa was expanded and doubled in size, with four intricately carved stone gateways depicting stories from the Buddha's life. Interestingly, on the gateways, the Buddha is not depicted in human form but represented by symbols such as footprints, the Bodhi tree, or the Dharma wheel.

cau_hoi: According to Chinese legend, which king successfully controlled the floods after 13 years and founded the Xia dynasty?
giai_thich: According to legend, Yu's father used the method of building dikes to block the water but failed. Yu used the method of dredging rivers and digging canals to lead the water to the sea. It is said that for 13 years, he passed by his home three times without entering. Due to his contributions, he was granted the throne and founded the Xia dynasty, the first dynasty recorded in Chinese history, although archaeologists still debate the existence of the Xia.

cau_hoi: The Yin ruins, the last capital of the Shang dynasty, where many oracle bone inscriptions were found, are located near which modern city?
giai_thich: Yin ruins mean "the remains of the Yin dynasty" (another name for the Shang dynasty), and were the capital around 1300 – 1046 BC. Excavations since 1928 have uncovered palaces, royal tombs, bronze artifacts, and tens of thousands of oracle bone fragments. This site is the first to prove the Shang dynasty's existence, not just a legend. The Yin ruins are a World Heritage site.

cau_hoi: Who is the famous female general of the Shang dynasty, wife of King Wu Ding, whose tomb was found intact in 1976?
giai_thich: Fu Hao was both a queen and a general commanding thousands of troops in many battles, as well as the presider of sacrificial ceremonies, which was rare for women at that time. Oracle bone inscriptions mention her about 170 – 200 times. Her tomb is the only royal tomb of the Shang dynasty that has not been looted, containing nearly 2,000 artifacts, including weapons, bronze items, and jade.

cau_hoi: Which concept was introduced by the Zhou dynasty to justify the overthrow of the Shang dynasty, claiming that heaven only grants the right to rule to virtuous people?
giai_thich: The Zhou believed that the last king of the Shang dynasty was cruel and thus lost the "Mandate of Heaven", and heaven granted the right to rule to the Zhou. This concept has been used throughout Chinese history: when disasters, famines, or uprisings occurred, people believed that the dynasty had lost the Mandate of Heaven, and the new dynasty had a legitimate reason to replace it.

cau_hoi: The Spring and Autumn period in China is named after which book?
A: The 'Spring and Autumn Annals', a chronicle of the State of Lu compiled by Confucius
C: A poem about spring and autumn
D: The agricultural calendar of the Zhou dynasty
giai_thich: The Spring and Autumn Annals records events of the State of Lu from 722 to 481 BC. Traditionally, it was compiled by Confucius, who selected each character to reflect praise and criticism. The name of the book derives from the two seasons of spring and autumn, indicating a whole year, thus 'chronicle'. The Spring and Autumn period lasted from about 770 to 476 BC, followed by the Warring States period.

cau_hoi: Which ancient Chinese book uses 64 hexagrams, each consisting of 6 solid or broken lines, for divination and reflection on change?
giai_thich: The Book of Changes (I Ching) originates from the Zhou dynasty and is one of the Five Classics of Confucianism. Each hexagram is made up of 6 yin (broken) or yang (solid) lines, creating 2^6 = 64 combinations. The German mathematician Leibniz, who developed the binary system used in computers, was amazed to find similarities between the hexagrams of the I Ching and his binary counting system.

cau_hoi: Which scholar proposed to Emperor Wu of Han to make Confucianism the state ideology?
giai_thich: Dong Zhongshu proposed to 'eliminate the hundred schools and exclusively promote Confucian teachings', meaning to use Confucianism in education and official appointments. In 124 BC, the Han established the Taixue, the first national university, teaching Confucian classics. From then on, Confucianism became the foundation of the Chinese government for about 2,000 years, until the early 20th century.

cau_hoi: Who was the female historian of the Eastern Han dynasty who completed the 'Book of Han' after her brother's death and wrote a book teaching women called 'Lessons for Women'?
giai_thich: Ban Zhao (circa 45 – 117) was the sister of historian Ban Gu and general Ban Chao. After Ban Gu died in prison, the emperor entrusted her to complete the Book of Han, especially the sections on astronomy and chronology. She also taught the empress and palace maids. She is the first known female historian of China. A volcano on Venus is named after her.

cau_hoi: The famous physician Hua Tuo of the late Eastern Han dynasty is known for using what in surgery, 1,600 years earlier than Europe?
giai_thich: Hua Tuo is believed to have mixed anesthetic with wine for patients to drink before surgery, called 'Mafitan', but the formula has been lost. He also created 'Five Animal Frolics', an exercise routine mimicking the movements of five animals (tiger, deer, bear, monkey, bird). According to legend, he was killed by Cao Cao for suggesting to operate on his head to cure a headache, which made Cao Cao suspicious.

cau_hoi: General Meng Tian of the Qin dynasty commanded 300,000 troops to extend the Great Wall against which nomadic people in the North?
giai_thich: The Xiongnu were a confederation of nomadic horse-riding tribes in the northern steppes, frequently attacking China's agricultural regions. Meng Tian drove the Xiongnu away and connected the old walls of the Warring States period into a long system. Legend has it that he improved the brush pen. He was forced to commit suicide after the death of Qin Shi Huang.

cau_hoi: The 'Bent Pyramid' at Dahshur, with a changing slope, was built for which pharaoh?
giai_thich: Sneferu is the father of Khufu, who built more pyramids than any other pharaoh. The Bent Pyramid was originally built with a slope of about 54 degrees, but halfway through, the architects had to reduce the angle to about 43 degrees, perhaps due to fears of collapse. Later, Sneferu built the nearby Red Pyramid, the first pyramid with a perfect flat surface.

cau_hoi: The Great Sphinx of Giza is believed by many archaeologists to bear the face of which pharaoh?
giai_thich: Khafre is the son of Khufu, who built the second pyramid at Giza. His pyramid appears taller than his father's because it was built on higher ground and still retains part of its casing stone at the top. The Sphinx is located near the road leading to Khafre's temple, so many archaeologists believe it was carved during his reign.

cau_hoi: Which is the smallest pyramid among the three large pyramids at Giza belonging to which pharaoh?
giai_thich: The Pyramid of Menkaure is only about 65 meters tall, less than half of Khufu's. The lower part is covered with red granite brought from Aswan, over 800 km away. In 1196, a sultan attempted to destroy this pyramid but gave up after 8 months due to the high costs, leaving only a large cut on the north face. A beautiful statue of Menkaure and his queen is now in Boston (USA).

cau_hoi: In Egyptian hieroglyphs, the names of kings and queens are written within an oval frame. What is this frame called?
giai_thich: A cartouche is an oval shape with a knot at the bottom, symbolizing the king's power over everything the sun shines upon. It was the cartouches that helped Champollion decipher hieroglyphs: he knew these frames contained the names of kings and then compared the names Ptolemy and Cleopatra with the Greek version. Today, visitors to Egypt often buy cartouche pendants with their names inscribed.

cau_hoi: How many different types of scripts are written on the Rosetta Stone?
giai_thich: The stone records a decree from 196 BC by priests praising King Ptolemy V, written in hieroglyphs (used for religious purposes), Demotic (the everyday script of the Egyptians), and Ancient Greek (the language of the Ptolemaic court). Because scholars could read Greek, they were able to compare it to decode the other two scripts. The stone weighs about 760 kg.

cau_hoi: In which museum is the Rosetta Stone currently displayed?
giai_thich: French soldiers discovered the stone in 1799 near the town of Rosetta (Rashid) in the Nile Delta. After France lost to Britain in Egypt, under the Treaty of Alexandria in 1801, the stone was handed over to the British. Since 1802, it has been displayed at the British Museum and is the most visited artifact there. Egypt has repeatedly requested its return.

cau_hoi: What was the name of the new capital built by Pharaoh Akhenaten to worship the god Aten?
giai_thich: Akhetaten means "Horizon of Aten," built in a previously uninhabited desert area. The city may have had around 20,000 – 50,000 people. After Akhenaten's death, the city was abandoned only about 15 years after its construction. This allowed archaeologists to find an intact layout of an ancient Egyptian city, along with the bust of Nefertiti.

cau_hoi: What was the original name of Pharaoh Tutankhamun before he changed it to honor the god Amun?
giai_thich: Tutankhaten means "Living Image of Aten," as he was born during the reign of Akhenaten, who worshipped only Aten. When he ascended the throne as a child, his advisors restored the worship of the old gods, and he changed his name to Tutankhamun, "Living Image of Amun." The capital was also moved away from Amarna. DNA analysis suggests he may be Akhenaten's son.

cau_hoi: Which mysterious land did the female pharaoh Hatshepsut famously organize a trade expedition to in order to bring back frankincense?
giai_thich: Hatshepsut's fleet traveled along the Red Sea to Punt, possibly in the region of modern-day Eritrea – Somalia, bringing back gold, ebony, leopard skins, monkeys, and even live frankincense trees in pots. The expedition is detailed in carvings on her temple walls, including images of the plump queen of Punt. The exact location of Punt remains debated by scholars.

cau_hoi: Where is the beautiful multi-tiered mortuary temple of the female pharaoh Hatshepsut, set against a cliff, located?
giai_thich: The temple was designed by architect Senenmut with three tiers of terraces connected by ramps, harmonizing with the cliff behind, appearing very modern despite being around 3,500 years old. The temple is located on the west bank of the Nile, opposite Luxor. Reliefs depict Hatshepsut's divine birth and the expedition to Punt. Many of her images were later defaced by her successors.

cau_hoi: "Nilometer" of ancient Egyptians was used for what purpose?
A: Measuring the water level of the Nile to predict crops and set taxes
giai_thich: A nilometer was typically a staircase leading down to the river or a well with measurement markings on the wall. If the floodwaters were too low, crops would fail and famine could occur; if too high, villages would be flooded. Priests relied on the water level to predict crops, and the government set tax rates accordingly. The nilometer on Elephantine Island in Aswan still exists today.

cau_hoi: Who is the first known author in world history, a female priestess and poet from Mesopotamia?
giai_thich: Enheduanna was the daughter of King Sargon of Akkad, appointed by her father as the high priestess of the moon god in the city of Ur around 2300 BC. She composed many hymns for the goddess Inanna and signed her works, making her the first known author by name. Her poetry was copied by scribes many centuries after her death.

cau_hoi: Which code from the city of Ur is known to be older than the Code of Hammurabi by about 300 years?
giai_thich: The Code of Ur-Nammu (circa 2100 – 2050 BC) is the oldest known legal code still in existence. Notably, many of the punishments in the code involve monetary compensation rather than physical retribution like Hammurabi's "eye for an eye." For example, breaking someone's bone would incur a specific fine. King Ur-Nammu was also responsible for building the large ziggurat at Ur.

cau_hoi: What are the giant bull or lion statues with human heads guarding the gates of the Assyrian palace called?
giai_thich: Lamassu is a protective deity, carved from massive stone blocks weighing around 30 tons. Many statues have five legs: when viewed from the front, two legs appear stationary, while from the side, four legs appear to be in motion, making them beautiful from all angles. Some of these statues are now in the British Museum and the Louvre. In 2015, lamassu statues still in Iraq were destroyed by a terrorist group.

cau_hoi: According to the Bible, which prophet led the Jews out of slavery in Egypt?
giai_thich: The Exodus story recounts how Moses demanded Pharaoh to free the Jews, and after ten plagues struck Egypt, Pharaoh agreed. The Red Sea parted for them to cross, then closed, drowning the pursuing Egyptian army. They wandered in the desert for 40 years before reaching the promised land. The Jewish Passover commemorates this event. Archaeologists still debate the historical accuracy of the story.

cau_hoi: According to the Bible, on which mountain did Moses receive the Ten Commandments from God?
giai_thich: Traditionally, the Ten Commandments were inscribed on two stone tablets, including prohibitions against murder, theft, and honoring parents. Mount Sinai is often identified with Jebel Musa in the Sinai Peninsula (Egypt), home to St. Catherine's Monastery, one of the oldest active Christian monasteries. Mount Ararat is believed to be where Noah's Ark came to rest.

cau_hoi: Which language was used as the common administrative language in the Achaemenid Persian Empire, and later became the language of Jesus?
giai_thich: Aramaic has a simple alphabet and spread throughout the Middle East since the Assyrian period. The Persian Empire used it for administrative texts across its territory from Egypt to India. Both square Hebrew and Arabic scripts developed from Aramaic. Today, there are still small communities in Syria and Iraq that speak modern Aramaic dialects.

cau_hoi: Who deciphered cuneiform script thanks to the trilingual inscription on the Behistun rock in Iran?
giai_thich: King Darius I had an inscription detailing his achievements carved in three languages (Old Persian, Elamite, and Babylonian) on a rock face about 100 meters above the ground. British officer Henry Rawlinson had to hang precariously on the cliff to copy it, sometimes assisted by a Kurdish boy. The Behistun inscription served as a key to cuneiform script, much like the Rosetta Stone did for hieroglyphs.

cau_hoi: Where is the simple tomb of Cyrus the Great, which Alexander the Great visited and respected, located?
giai_thich: Pasargadae was the first capital established by Cyrus. His tomb is a small stone chamber on six steps, very modest compared to his power. Historians say that when Alexander saw the tomb vandalized, he was very angry and ordered repairs. Legend has it that the inscription on the tomb reminds viewers not to envy the small piece of land covering his body.

cau_hoi: In 330 BC, which city in Persia had its palace burned by Alexander the Great's forces?
giai_thich: Ancient historians provide various reasons: it may have been revenge for Persia burning Athens 150 years earlier, or it could have been an impulsive act during a party. Alexander is said to have regretted this act. The fire destroyed wooden buildings but helped preserve thousands of clay tablets of administrative records, aiding our understanding of how the Persian Empire operated.

cau_hoi: Which scholar in ancient India (around the 4th century BC) wrote a Sanskrit grammar consisting of nearly 4,000 concise rules, regarded as one of the greatest linguistic works?
giai_thich: Pāṇini described the entire grammar of Sanskrit in about 3,959 very brief rules, similar to formulas. His method of using rules to create correct sentences resembles how computer scientists today describe programming languages. A notation method in computer science is even called "Backus-Naur-Pāṇini form" in his honor.

cau_hoi: The physician Sushruta in ancient India is famous for which surgical technique, considered a precursor to cosmetic surgery?
A: Nose reconstruction using skin from the cheek or forehead
giai_thich: The "Sushruta Samhita" describes over 300 surgical procedures and more than 120 instruments. At that time, nose cutting was a common punishment, making nose reconstruction techniques very necessary. In the late 18th century, British doctors in India witnessed this technique and brought it back to Europe, contributing to the development of modern plastic surgery. Sushruta is often referred to as the "father of surgery."

cau_hoi: The fortress atop the massive rock Sigiriya ("Lion Rock") in Sri Lanka was built by which king in the 5th century?
giai_thich: Kashyapa I seized the throne by killing his father, fearing revenge from his brother, and built a palace atop a rock about 200 meters high. The ascent passes through two giant lion's paws, which still remain today. The rock features murals of maidens and the "Mirror Wall" that was once polished to a shine. Sigiriya is a World Heritage Site.

cau_hoi: Why is the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi tree in Anuradhapura (Sri Lanka) world-famous?
A: It is the oldest recorded human-planted tree in the world
B: It is the largest fruit-bearing tree in the world
C: It is the tallest tree in the world
D: It is the only tree that grows underwater
giai_thich: The tree was planted in 288 BC from a branch of the Bodhi tree in Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha attained enlightenment, brought by the nun Sanghamitta, the daughter of King Ashoka. The kings of Sri Lanka have cared for the tree for over 2,300 years, with guardianship passed down through generations. The original tree in Bodh Gaya has been cut down, making the tree in Sri Lanka a precious "descendant."

cau_hoi: "Hong Mon Yen", a dangerous banquet where one side intends to assassinate the other, was a meeting between whom?
A: Qin Shi Huang and Jing Ke
giai_thich: In 206 BC, Liu Bang entered Handan (the capital of Qin) first, angering Xiang Yu. Liu Bang went to Hong Mon to apologize. During the banquet, Xiang Yu's strategist Fan Zeng signaled to kill Liu Bang, and Xiang Yu brandished a sword intending to stab, but hesitated. Liu Bang took the opportunity to excuse himself to escape. "Hong Mon Yen" now refers to meetings with dangerous plots.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the oldest anthology of poetry in China, consisting of 305 poems from the Western Zhou to the Spring and Autumn period?
giai_thich: The Book of Songs includes folk songs, court songs, and sacrificial songs, composed around the 11th to 6th centuries BC. Traditionally, Confucius selected 305 poems from about 3,000. Confucius taught his students that without studying the Book of Songs, one would not know how to speak properly. The opening poem "Guan Shu" about the cuckoo by the riverside is a famous love poem.

cau_hoi: The Duanwu Festival with the tradition of dragon boat racing and zongzi wrapping is believed to commemorate which poet?
giai_thich: Qu Yuan (circa 340 – 278 BC) was a loyal minister of the State of Chu, slandered and exiled. Upon hearing that the capital was captured by the Qin army, he embraced a stone and drowned himself in the Miluo River on the 5th day of the 5th lunar month. According to legend, the people rowed boats to search for him and threw wrapped rice into the river so that fish would not eat his body. He is considered the first known poet of China.

cau_hoi: Which philosopher of the Warring States period advocated "universal love", meaning to love everyone equally, and opposed aggressive wars?
giai_thich: Mozi believed that if everyone loved others as they loved themselves, there would be no war. Unlike Confucius, who emphasized rituals, he advocated frugality and opposed extravagant funerals. His students were also skilled engineers in city defense, ready to help smaller states resist invasion. The first quantum satellite of China in 2016 was named "Mozi".

cau_hoi: Who was the last native pharaoh of ancient Egypt before being ruled by the Persians and then the Greeks?
giai_thich: Nectanebo II belonged to the 30th dynasty, defeated by the Persians in 343 BC and fled south. After him, Egypt was ruled by the Persians, then Alexander the Great, and the Greek Ptolemies. It was not until over 2,000 years later, in the 20th century, that Egypt had a native Egyptian leader again. Cleopatra VII belonged to the Greek Ptolemaic dynasty.

cau_hoi: Which pharaoh expelled the Hyksos from Egypt, marking the beginning of the New Kingdom?
giai_thich: Around 1550 BC, Ahmose I advanced from Thebes to the north, capturing the Hyksos capital Avaris and driving them back to Canaan. His father and brother had died in previous battles. The mummy of his father, King Seqenenre Tao, showed head wounds indicating he died in battle. Ahmose I established the 18th dynasty, the dynasty of Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, and Tutankhamun.

cau_hoi: Which Egyptian stele, around 1208 BC, contains the earliest known mention of the name "Israel"?
giai_thich: Pharaoh Merneptah, son of Ramses II, had a stele inscribed recording his victories, including the phrase "Israel is laid waste, its seed is no more." This is the earliest non-biblical evidence mentioning a group called Israel in Canaan. British archaeologist Flinders Petrie discovered the stele in 1896, and it is now housed in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

cau_hoi: What is the most famous mathematical document of ancient Egypt, containing 84 problems about fractions, areas, and volumes, called?
giai_thich: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus was written around 1550 BC by the scribe Ahmes, copied from an older version. It is named after Alexander Henry Rhind, a Scotsman who bought it in Luxor in 1858. The document contains practical problems such as dividing bread among many people or calculating the slope of a pyramid. The Egyptians used an approximate value of pi around 3.16.

cau_hoi: The Amarna Letters, a collection of diplomatic correspondence between pharaohs and foreign kings found in Egypt, were written in which script?
giai_thich: In 1887, an Egyptian peasant woman dug in Amarna and found about 380 clay tablets. These were letters between pharaohs (such as Akhenaten) and kings of Babylon, Assyria, Hittite, and vassal kings in Canaan, written in cuneiform and primarily in Akkadian. In the letters, the kings referred to each other as "brothers" and demanded gifts of gold.

cau_hoi: The Ishtar Gate of Babylon, reconstructed with original glazed bricks, is currently located in which museum?
giai_thich: German archaeologists excavated Babylon from 1899 to 1917 and brought thousands of glazed brick fragments to Berlin. It took many years to piece them together, and the gate was displayed from 1930. Due to the original gate's size, the museum only reconstructed a small front section. In Iraq, at the ruins of Babylon, there is a replica of the gate.

cau_hoi: Which museum currently displays the stone stele inscribed with the Code of Hammurabi?
giai_thich: In 1901, a French archaeological team discovered the stele in the city of Susa (Iran), where the Elamites had brought it back as a trophy around 1158 BC. The black basalt stele, which was broken into three pieces, was reassembled. Part of the inscription on the front was worn away by the Elamites, possibly to engrave the name of their king, but this was never accomplished.

cau_hoi: Among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, which wonder is still uncertain to have actually existed?
giai_thich: Other wonders have archaeological evidence or descriptions from contemporaries. However, the Hanging Gardens are only mentioned by Greek authors many centuries later, while Babylonian texts, including those of Nebuchadnezzar II, do not mention them. Researcher Stephanie Dalley suggests that the gardens were actually in Nineveh, built by Assyrian king Sennacherib, and may have been confused.

cau_hoi: Approximately how many clay tablets and fragments were found in the library of King Ashurbanipal in Nineveh?
giai_thich: About 30,000 clay tablets and fragments were found, containing literature, medicine, astronomy, divination, and dictionaries. Ashurbanipal ordered the collection and copying of every valuable text in the empire. In 1872, while studying the tablets at the British Museum, George Smith discovered a story about a great flood similar to the Biblical account, and it is said he was so moved that he stripped off his clothes in the room.

cau_hoi: How long was the Royal Road of the Persian Empire, connecting Susa to Sardis?
giai_thich: The road was about 2,700 km long and had around 111 rest stations, each with replacement horses, water, and food. Pedestrians typically took about 90 days, but the mounted courier system only took about 7 to 9 days. The road allowed the king to quickly receive news and deploy troops throughout the empire. Many sections were reused during the Roman period.

cau_hoi: According to Herodotus, which queen of the nomadic Massagetae did Cyrus the Great die fighting against?
giai_thich: Cyrus used a ruse to capture the queen Tomyris's son, who then committed suicide. Tomyris attacked, defeated the Persian army, and killed Cyrus in 530 BC. According to Herodotus's account, she dipped Cyrus's head into a bowl of blood and said, "I promised you a drink of blood to your heart's content." Other historians have different accounts of Cyrus's death.

cau_hoi: Which nomadic people of the steppe are famous for their gold jewelry shaped like animals and burying their leaders in large burial mounds (kurgan)?
giai_thich: The Scythians lived on the steppe from the Black Sea to Siberia from around the 9th to the 2nd century BC. They were skilled horse archers. Their gold artifacts depict deer, leopards, and eagles with many curvilinear designs. In Siberia, archaeologists have found naturally mummified remains in ice of a woman, the "Altai Princess," with animal tattoos still visible.

cau_hoi: In 200 BC, which Xiongnu Chanyu besieged Han Gaozu Liu Bang for 7 days at Baideng (near Datong, China)?
giai_thich: Mao Dun unified the Xiongnu tribes into a powerful nomadic empire. He besieged Liu Bang at Baideng Mountain (Baideng, different from the Bach Dang River in Vietnam), and Liu Bang only escaped by bribing the Chanyu's wife. Later, the Han had to follow a policy of "marriage alliance": marrying a princess and gifting silk, wine, and rice to the Xiongnu annually.

cau_hoi: Wang Zhaojun, one of the "Four Great Beauties" of China, was married off by the Han to whom to maintain peace?
giai_thich: In 33 BC, Zhaojun was a palace maid who had never met the emperor. According to legend, because she did not bribe the artist to paint her portrait, she was depicted poorly. When the Xiongnu Chanyu requested to marry a Han girl, she volunteered to go. Only at the farewell did the emperor realize her beauty and deeply regretted it. She contributed to about 60 years of peace between the two sides.

cau_hoi: Which general of the Eastern Han restored control over the Western Regions and is famous for the saying "You can't catch tiger cubs without entering the tiger's den"?
giai_thich: Ban Zhao, the brother of historian Ban Gu, originally worked as a hired scribe but threw down his pen to join the army. When he was sent as an envoy to a kingdom in the Western Regions, he had only 36 men but attacked the Xiongnu envoy's camp at night, forcing the king of that place to submit to the Han. He spent about 30 years in the Western Regions, bringing over 50 kingdoms under Han control, and only returned home when he was over 70 years old.

cau_hoi: In 97, Ban Zhao sent the envoy Gan Ying to the Roman Empire. Where did Gan Ying turn back?
giai_thich: Gan Ying reached the coast, possibly the Persian Gulf or the region of Mesopotamia. The Parthians, who were mediating silk trade and did not want China to contact Rome directly, told him that crossing the sea would take from 3 months to 2 years and many people died from homesickness. Gan Ying became discouraged and turned back. This was the closest the Han Chinese came to Rome that we know of.

cau_hoi: What name did the ancient Romans use to refer to China, the land of silk production?
giai_thich: "Seres" means "people who make silk," derived from the Greek word "ser" (silk). The Romans highly valued silk but did not know how it was made; some even thought silk grew on trees. Silk was so expensive that the Roman Senate once tried to ban men from wearing it, considering it a luxury. The secret of silkworm cultivation only reached Europe in the 6th century when monks hid silkworm eggs in bamboo sticks to bring back to Constantinople.

cau_hoi: "The Book of Han" holds what special significance in the history of Chinese historiography?
A: It is the first history written in Latin
C: It is the first printed book
D: It is the first history written solely about one dynasty
giai_thich: Unlike Sima Qian's "Records of the Grand Historian," which covers thousands of years of history, "The Book of Han" focuses only on the Western Han dynasty. This writing style became a model for the "Twenty-Four Histories," the 24 official histories of later Chinese dynasties. The book was initiated by Ban Biao, largely written by his son Ban Gu, and completed by his daughter Ban Zhao.

cau_hoi: Which powerful eunuch of the Qin dynasty tested the loyalty of officials by saying "this deer is a horse"?
giai_thich: After the death of Qin Shi Huang, Zhao Gao and Li Si forged an edict to place Hu Hai on the throne. To see who dared to oppose him, Zhao Gao brought a deer into the court and claimed it was a horse. Those officials who dared to speak the truth that it was a deer were subsequently harmed. The idiom "pointing at a deer and calling it a horse" now refers to deliberately distorting the truth. Zhao Gao was later executed.

cau_hoi: Which script did the Chancellor Li Si of the Qin dynasty standardize across China?
giai_thich: Before the Qin dynasty, each state had its own writing system. Li Si simplified and unified it into Small Seal Script, characterized by regular curved strokes. This standardization of writing allowed people from different dialect regions to understand the same texts, maintaining cultural unity in China. The seal script is still used today for engraving seals.

cau_hoi: In addition to writing and measurement units, the Qin dynasty also standardized the distance between two wheels (axles). What was the main purpose?
B: To make carts run faster than horses
C: To allow carts to travel on deep ruts on all roads
D: To distinguish between noble and commoner carts
giai_thich: The dirt roads of that time had deep ruts created by wheels. If the distance between wheels varied from place to place, carts from one region would struggle on the roads of another. Standardizing the axle width facilitated the transport of goods and troops throughout the empire. This policy is known as "same axle, same script" (vehicles with the same axle, books with the same characters).

cau_hoi: What is the most famous part of the Mahabharata, the dialogue between Prince Arjuna and God Krishna before the battle, called?
giai_thich: Before the great battle at Kurukshetra, Arjuna was distressed about fighting against his own relatives and teachers. God Krishna, acting as his charioteer, explained duty, selfless action, and the nature of the soul. The Bhagavad Gita consists of 700 verses and is one of the most important texts in Hinduism. Gandhi referred to it as his "spiritual dictionary."

cau_hoi: The Indian mathematician Brahmagupta (7th century) is famous for being the first to introduce calculation rules involving which concept?
giai_thich: In 628, Brahmagupta wrote a book outlining rules such as "a number added to 0 remains itself" and "multiplying a negative number by a negative number yields a positive number." He referred to positive numbers as "assets" and negative numbers as "debts." He was the first to treat 0 as a real number for calculations, rather than just a placeholder. However, he still misunderstood division by 0.

cau_hoi: The ancient academic center of Taxila, where Chanakya is said to have taught, is located in which modern-day country?
giai_thich: Taxila is located near Pakistan's capital Islamabad, at the crossroads of trade routes between India, Central Asia, and Persia. From around the 6th century BC, scholars came here to teach medicine, law, military science, and the Vedas. Alexander the Great visited Taxila in 326 BC. The ruins here show the influence of many cultures: Persian, Greek, Indian, and Buddhist.

cau_hoi: In 326 BC, at the Battle of the Hydaspes River in Punjab, which Indian king did Alexander the Great defeat?
giai_thich: King Porus fought with around 200 war elephants, posing significant challenges for the Macedonian army. According to historians, after Porus was captured, Alexander asked him how he wished to be treated, to which Porus replied, "Like a king." Alexander admired him and allowed him to continue ruling his kingdom. Alexander's beloved horse Bucephalus died after this battle, and he founded a city in its name.

cau_hoi: At which river bank did Alexander the Great's soldiers refuse to advance further into India, forcing him to turn back?
giai_thich: After 8 years of campaigning and traveling tens of thousands of kilometers, the Macedonian soldiers were exhausted, homesick, and heard tales of kingdoms ahead with thousands of war elephants. Alexander, furious, locked himself in his tent for three days but ultimately had to agree to turn back. On the return journey through the Gedrosia desert, many soldiers died of thirst. Alexander died in Babylon just about three years later.

cau_hoi: According to historians, what did Seleucus I (the general who succeeded Alexander) receive in exchange for eastern territories when he made peace with Chandragupta Maurya?
giai_thich: Around 305 – 303 BC, after a war, Seleucus ceded present-day Afghanistan and Pakistan to Chandragupta. In return, he received 500 war elephants. These elephants played a crucial role in the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BC, helping Seleucus defeat his western rivals. The two sides may have also arranged a marriage between the two royal families.

cau_hoi: The city of Meroë in the ancient Kingdom of Kush in Sudan is famous for which industry, earning it the nickname "the Birmingham of Africa"?
giai_thich: Meroë had abundant iron ore and wood for charcoal. The Kushites engaged in large-scale iron smelting, and archaeologists have found massive piles of iron slag around the city. Birmingham was the famous industrial city in England during the Industrial Revolution. Meroë was the capital of Kush from around the 3rd century BC to the 4th century, and it had its own script that has not been fully deciphered.

cau_hoi: Which Pharaoh of Egypt is believed to have reigned the longest in history, possibly around 90 years, ascending to the throne at about 6 years old?
giai_thich: According to ancient king lists, Pepi II of the Old Kingdom reigned for about 90 years (around 2278 – 2184 BC), although some scholars suggest the actual number may be shorter. A letter from him as a child shows he was very eager to see a dancing dwarf brought from the south. Ramses II reigned for about 66 years.

cau_hoi: The first recorded strike in history occurred in Egypt around 1157 BC. What profession did the strikers belong to?
B: Masons and decorators of royal tombs
giai_thich: During the reign of Ramses III, craftsmen in the village of Deir el-Medina, who carved and painted tombs in the Valley of the Kings, did not receive their wheat rations on time. They stopped working and sat in front of the temples, saying "We are hungry!". A scribe recorded the event on papyrus. Eventually, they received their rations, showing that the strike was successful.

cau_hoi: A copy of the peace treaty between Egypt and the Hittites (around 1259 BC) is displayed where today as a symbol of peace?
D: The United Nations Headquarters in New York
giai_thich: The Treaty of Kadesh is considered one of the oldest known peace treaties whose content is still known. It includes terms of non-aggression, mutual assistance when attacked, and the return of refugees, similar to modern treaties. Turkey donated an enlarged replica of the Hittite clay tablet to the United Nations, which is displayed at its New York headquarters.

cau_hoi: Which ancient city in Syria is where one of the oldest alphabets in the world, with 30 letters written in cuneiform, was found?
giai_thich: Ugarit was a wealthy port city on the Syrian coast, destroyed around 1185 BC. In 1928, a farmer plowing his field accidentally broke into an ancient tomb, leading to the excavation of the city. The Ugaritians used cuneiform, but each symbol represented only one sound, like an alphabet. Here, one of the oldest pieces of music in the world, the "Hurrian Hymn," was also found.

cau_hoi: According to Herodotus, which Pharaoh ordered Phoenician sailors to sail around Africa around 600 BC?
giai_thich: According to the account, the journey took about 3 years; they set out from the Red Sea, traveled south, and returned through the Strait of Gibraltar. Herodotus did not believe one detail: they claimed that when sailing around the southern tip of Africa, the Sun was on their right side (the north). However, this detail suggests they may have actually traveled into the Southern Hemisphere, leading many scholars to believe the story could be true.

cau_hoi: Which wealthy King Croesus of Lydia was defeated by whom in 546 BC?
giai_thich: According to Herodotus, Croesus consulted the oracle at Delphi about whether to attack Persia and was told: "If you cross the Halys River, a great empire will fall." Croesus thought it referred to the Persian Empire, but it actually referred to his own empire. Cyrus captured the capital, Sardis. This story is a famous example of prophecies that can be interpreted in two ways.

cau_hoi: The book "Anabasis" by the Greek historian Xenophon recounts the arduous retreat of whom?
A: 10,000 Greek mercenaries from Persia back home
C: The army of Alexander the Great
giai_thich: In 401 BC, about 10,000 Greek mercenaries were hired to help the Persian prince Cyrus the Younger seize the throne, but Cyrus was killed, and the Greek generals were tricked into being killed. Xenophon, then a young man, was elected as one of the commanders, leading them on foot thousands of kilometers through snowy mountains to the Black Sea. Upon seeing the sea, they shouted "Thalatta! Thalatta!" (The Sea! The Sea!).

cau_hoi: The Greek-Bactrian Kingdom, established by the descendants of Alexander's soldiers, was primarily located in which region today?
giai_thich: After Alexander's death, many Greeks remained in Bactria (northern Afghanistan). Around 250 BC, they established their own kingdom, building Greek-style cities with theaters and gymnasiums, such as Ai-Khanoum. They minted beautiful coins depicting their kings. This is an example of Greek cultural fusion deep in Central Asia.

cau_hoi: Which Greek-Indian king is said to have converted to Buddhism after a philosophical dialogue with the monk Nagasena, recorded in the book "Milinda's Questions"?
giai_thich: King Menander I ruled the Punjab and Gandhara around the 2nd century BC. In the book, the king poses difficult questions about the soul and reincarnation, and the monk Nagasena responds with easy-to-understand examples, such as comparing a person to a chariot made up of many parts. The book is an important text of Theravada Buddhism. This is an intriguing encounter between Greek thought and Buddhism.

cau_hoi: Who deciphered the Brahmi script on the inscriptions of King Ashoka in 1837?
giai_thich: For centuries, no one in India could read the inscriptions on Ashoka's stone pillars. James Prinsep, a mint official in Calcutta, compared the symbols on coins and inscriptions, and successfully deciphered them in 1837. Thanks to this, the world came to know about the great King Ashoka, who had previously been nearly forgotten. The Brahmi script is the ancestor of most scripts in India and Southeast Asia today.

cau_hoi: In which Indian state is the ancient port city of Lothal, which may have the oldest shipyard in the world, located?
giai_thich: Lothal was built around 2400 BC and features a large brick dock connected to the river, which many archaeologists believe was a shipyard for boats to enter and exit. The city was a center for bead production and trade with Mesopotamia, where beads and Indus seals have been found. Lothal means "Mound of the Dead" in Gujarati, similar to the meaning of Mohenjo-daro.

cau_hoi: Which animal appears most frequently on the seals of the Indus Valley Civilization?
giai_thich: About 60-70% of Indus seals depict a bovine-like creature, viewed from the side, with only one horn, standing in front of what looks like a feeding trough or altar. Archaeologists jokingly call it a "unicorn." It may be a cow depicted in profile, hence only one horn is visible, or it could be a mythical creature. Its true significance remains a mystery as the script has not been deciphered.

cau_hoi: The famous Sanxingdui site with its strange bulging-eyed bronze masks and large ears is located in which province of China?
giai_thich: Sanxingdui, near Chengdu, dates back to around 1200-1000 BC, contemporary with the Shang dynasty. In 1986, archaeologists discovered two pits containing hundreds of bronze, gold, jade, and ivory artifacts, including a 2.6-meter tall bronze figure and masks with bulging cylindrical eyes. The style is very different from the Central Plains culture, indicating a distinct civilization that historical records barely mention.

cau_hoi: In the Battle of Changping in 260 BC, one of the bloodiest battles of ancient times, which state did Qin defeat?
giai_thich: The State of Zhao replaced the cautious old general Lian Po with Zhao Kuo, a young man who was only skilled in theoretical military strategy from books. The Zhao army was besieged by the Qin general Bai Qi and cut off from supplies for 46 days. According to historical records, about 400,000 Zhao soldiers surrendered and were killed. The idiom "strategizing on paper" (only knowing theory) originates from Zhao Kuo.

cau_hoi: Which famous assassin attempted to kill King Qin (later known as Qin Shi Huang) in 227 BC with a dagger hidden in a scroll?
giai_thich: The prince of Yan sent Jing Ke to present a map of Yan and the head of a general who opposed Qin as a gift to the Qin king. When he opened the scroll, the hidden poisoned dagger was revealed, and Jing Ke seized it and stabbed, but the Qin king dodged and ran around a pillar. No one was allowed to bring weapons into the palace, so a court physician threw a medicine pouch at Jing Ke. In the end, the king drew his sword to fight back, and Jing Ke was killed.

cau_hoi: What did the alchemist Xu Fu, sent by Qin Shi Huang to the eastern sea with thousands of young men and women, seek?
giai_thich: Qin Shi Huang was very afraid of death and wanted to live forever. Xu Fu claimed that there were immortal herbs on the mythical Penglai Mountain in the sea. He set off with a large fleet but never returned. There are legends that he reached Japan and settled there, and many places in Japan worship Xu Fu. Ironically, Qin Shi Huang may have died from taking a "longevity" potion that contained mercury.

cau_hoi: Who was the empress of Liu Bang, the founder of the Han Dynasty, who held real power in the court for about 15 years after his death?
giai_thich: Empress Lü was the first woman to hold power in unified China. She was intelligent, decisive, and ruthless towards her opponents. However, during her reign, the country was relatively stable, taxes were reduced, helping the people recover after the war. After her death in 180 BC, the high officials eliminated the Lü family to restore the Liu family to power.

cau_hoi: Which dynasty is associated with the prosperous period known as "Wenjing's Rule", characterized by light taxation and a wealthy populace?
giai_thich: Emperor Wen of Han and Emperor Jing of Han (180-141 BC) followed Daoist principles of "wu wei", significantly lowering land taxes, reducing punishments, and living frugally. Emperor Wen was famous for wearing coarse clothing and not building additional palaces. According to historical records, by the end of this period, granaries were so full that old grains rotted, and the money in the treasury had not been used for so long that the strings of coins broke.

cau_hoi: "The Rebellion of the Seven States", the uprising of seven vassal kingdoms against the Han dynasty, occurred in which year?
giai_thich: During the reign of Emperor Jing of Han, the high official Chen Fan proposed reducing the land of the vassal kings. Seven kings, led by the king of Wu, revolted, claiming to "kill Chen Fan to purify the court". The emperor ordered Chen Fan's execution, but the kings did not withdraw their troops. General Zhu Ahfu quelled the rebellion in about three months, consolidating central power.

cau_hoi: The three sworn brothers in "The Peach Garden" from the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms are Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and who?
giai_thich: According to the novel, the three swore in the peach garden that "they do not need to be born on the same day, only hope to die on the same day". Liu Bei is the eldest brother, Guan Yu is the second brother, and Zhang Fei is the youngest. Guan Yu was later revered as "Guan Gong", the god of loyalty, and has temples dedicated to him in many places, including Vietnam. The peach garden oath scene is a fictional detail from the novel.

cau_hoi: Who unified China in 280, ending the Three Kingdoms period and establishing the Western Jin dynasty?
giai_thich: Sima Yan was the grandson of Sima Yi, a high official of the Wei dynasty who was a rival of Zhuge Liang. In 265, he forced the Wei emperor to abdicate and established the Jin dynasty, then in 280 destroyed the Wu state, unifying China. However, after his death, the Sima princes fought in the "Rebellion of the Eight Princes", causing the country to fall back into division.

cau_hoi: In the Epic of Gilgamesh, what is the name of Gilgamesh's close friend, initially a wild man created by the gods?
giai_thich: The gods created Enkidu from clay to be a worthy opponent for the arrogant Gilgamesh. After a wrestling match, the two became close friends and together killed the monster Humbaba who guarded the cedar forest. When Enkidu was punished by the gods and died, Gilgamesh was heartbroken and began his journey to seek immortality. This is one of the oldest friendship stories in literature.

cau_hoi: In the Epic of Gilgamesh, which character survived the great flood by building a large boat, similar to the story of Noah?
giai_thich: Utnapishtim was warned by the god Ea about the flood, so he built a large boat, taking his family and various animals aboard. After seven days of rain, the boat came to rest on a mountain. He released a dove, a swallow, and then a raven to see if the waters had receded, very similar to the story in the Bible. The gods granted him immortality, and Gilgamesh came to ask for his secret.

cau_hoi: The famous Babylonian clay tablet known as Plimpton 322, approximately 3,800 years old, contains which mathematical content?
giai_thich: The tablet has 15 rows of numbers, listing integer triples such as (3, 4, 5) that satisfy the theorem about right triangles, which is about 1,000 years before Pythagoras. Some researchers even believe this is an ancient trigonometric table. The tablet is named after publisher George Plimpton, who donated it to Columbia University (New York), where it is preserved.

cau_hoi: The ancient bronze machine found in a shipwreck in Greece in 1901, often referred to as "the world's oldest analog computer", is called what?
giai_thich: The Antikythera mechanism was made around the 2nd – 1st century BC, consisting of at least 30 intricate bronze gears. When the handle is turned, it can predict the positions of the Sun, Moon, planets, eclipses, and even the schedule of the Olympic Games. Devices of similar complexity did not appear in Europe until about 1,000 years later. Scientists used X-rays to study its interior.

cau_hoi: Which inventor in Alexandria in the 1st century described a spinning ball powered by steam, considered the first primitive steam engine?
giai_thich: Hero's "aeolipile" spins when the water in the pot is boiled and steam shoots out from two curved pipes. However, it was only used as a toy or display item in temples. Hero also designed self-opening temple doors, an automatic holy water dispenser using coins, and an automatic puppet theater. It took about 1,700 years for steam engines to be used in industry.

cau_hoi: Which famous female mathematician, astronomer, and philosopher from Alexandria was killed by a mob in 415?
giai_thich: Hypatia was the daughter of the mathematician Theon, teaching philosophy and mathematics to students of various religions. She wrote commentaries on geometry and astronomy and is believed to have improved the design of the astronomical instrument astrolabe. She became embroiled in political and religious conflicts in Alexandria and was brutally murdered. She is often regarded as the first female mathematician recorded in history.

cau_hoi: Which ancient royal library was established by King Ashurbanipal in the 7th century BC, housing thousands of cuneiform clay tablets including the Epic of Gilgamesh?
giai_thich: Ashurbanipal was the last great king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, renowned not only for his military prowess but also for his deep love of knowledge. He ordered the collection and copying of all religious, scientific, and literary texts throughout Mesopotamia to his capital Nineveh. 19th-century archaeologists discovered over 30,000 clay tablets here, opening a priceless treasure trove that helps humanity understand the ancient world.
